#7918. Pyometra: Signs, Causes, and Care (Vet Answer)

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Your female dog is drinking more, panting, lethargic, and you know something just isnât right. Never ignore that feeling. You know your dog better than anyone else, and if you think something is wrong, it probably is. And if your dog hasnât been spayed, you could be seeing signs of pyometra: infection of the womb or uterus that can turn deadly if left untreated.

Any dog with a uterus can develop a uterine infection, and, although rare, even dogs that have had a laparoscopic or âkeyholeâ spay, where only the ovaries are removed, can be at risk of pyometra. So, what is pyometra? Read on to find out.

An infected uterus or womb, sometimes referred to in practice as a âpyoâ, is a relatively common condition affecting entire female dogs. It occurs most commonly in middle-aged to older dogs, but cases have been reported in dogs as young as 9 months.

In dogs, the uterus splits into two branches or âhornsâ that allow multiple fetuses to be carried on each side. Female dogs come into season or estrus around every six months once they reach sexual maturity. This is when she becomes fertile and receptive to mating. If she becomes pregnant, all being well, she will deliver a litter of puppies approximately 63 days later. Sometimes there can be a âphantomâ or âfalseâ pregnancy, also known as pseudopregnancy, where the fluctuating hormones surrounding estrus and mating prepare the dog for pregnancy, even when fertilization hasnât occurred.

Every time a dog goes through estrus, her cervix relaxes and opens, and the lining of the uterus thickens in preparation for mating and pregnancy. Ordinarily, the cervix helps prevent dirt, debris, and harmful bacteria from entering the uterus, so when the cervix is open, the risk of contamination and infection increases. If fluid and bacteria accumulate, infection can set in over the following 2-3 weeks, resulting in pyometra.

There are two types of pyometra: open and closed.

The more common and less dangerous of the two, an open pyometra occurs when there is infection in the uterus, but the cervix remains open. Dogs with an open pyometra are often diagnosed more easily because owners notice a foul-smelling discharge coming from the vulva, or that their dog becomes obsessed with licking her nether regions.

Because the pus can drain out of the uterus, an open pyometra tends to be less of a threat than one that is closed. However, an open pyometra can become closed, and vice versa.

A closed pyometra occurs when the cervix has shut, locking infection inside the body. It is a far more dangerous situation because the problem is not always immediately obvious, and, as the infection continues, pus fills and stretches the uterus. This can bring a risk of septicemia (infection of the bloodstream) and uterine rupture, both of which carry a high risk of mortality.

The signs of pyometra usually appear around 2-3 weeks after estrus. As mentioned above, dogs with an open pyometra may have a yellow, greenish, or brown discharge from the vulva which, if you get close enough to discover, smells pretty awful. However, dogs that are quite clean may lick up any discharge before you notice, so itâs important to be aware of the other signs of pyometra, which include:

With each season a dog experiences, her risk of uterine infection increases. At each estrus, the cervix opens, and the repeated thickening of the uterine wall reduces its ability to contract and expel fluid and contaminants. Dogs over 7 years old are typically at higher risk, but pyometra can affect even young dogs.

The most common bacteria involved in pyometra is Escherichia coli (E. coli), responsible for around 90% of cases, usually from fecal contamination.1 Obesity, recessed vulvas, chronic diarrhea, and thick coats that regularly become soiled increase the incidence of fecal contamination of the vagina and uterus, putting dogs at a much greater risk for pyometra.

Studies have also shown that diet can affect the growth of pathogenic E. coli and therefore influence pyometra risk.2

The use of synthetic hormones to prevent embryo implantation or induce abortion in the case of accidental mating, or to suppress or delay estrus, has also been found to increase the risk of pyometra.3

Your vet will diagnose pyometra based on a combination of the history, clinical signs, and examination. They will usually perform a brief abdominal ultrasound. Pyometra appears as fluid inside the uterine horns, visible on ultrasound as discrete black circles or tubes.

pyometra in dogs,ultrasound findings and diagnosis

They will also perform some bloodwork to check for signs of septicemia and assess kidney function, hydration status, and rule out any other underlying issues.

The fastest and most definitive treatment of pyometra is to perform an ovariohysterectomy â spay the dog.

The first step in treating pyometra is to start antibiotic therapy and intravenous fluids. Depending on the severity of the situation, your vet may recommend that your dog stay overnight on these treatments before proceeding with surgery, or they may want to go ahead right away.

Occasionally, mild cases of pyometra can be successfully managed using a combination of hormonal treatments and antibiotics. However, dogs that have had one episode of pyometra have a much higher chance of having another, which is why surgery is usually recommended. Once the ovaries and uterus have been removed, a dog can never get pyometra again.

The surgical removal of the ovaries and uterus will completely eliminate the risk of pyometra. Dogs that are spayed earlier in life also have a significantly lower risk of mammary cancer.

In the last decade, advice regarding the timing of spaying has changed, and most vets recommend waiting until after the first season to ensure she has reached sexual maturity. For small breeds, the first season might occur at around 6 months, while for large or giant breeds, the first season may not happen until they are at least 12-18 months old.

In a keyhole or laparoscopic spay, only the ovaries are removed (ovariectomy); the uterus is left behind. This has become a popular option due to the perceived reduction in pain, discomfort, and recovery time. However, when performed on young, healthy dogs, the most challenging part of a routine spay is trying to convince the patient to stay quiet and calm after surgery!

Theoretically, by removing the hormonal factor, ovariectomy should prevent pyometra. However, in the case of ovarian remnant syndrome, where fragments of ovarian tissue are left behind, uterine infection can occur.

Breeding from a dog that has (or has had) pyometra is not recommended. The circumstances that allow pyometra to form â open cervix, thickened uterine walls, contamination â can also make pregnancy riskier for the dog.

Additionally, pyometra can damage the uterine lining, reducing fertility and increasing pregnancy risks.

Before surgical spaying became common practice, allowing dogs to mate and have litters was likely seen as the best way to avoid pyometra. This is probably where the old wivesâ tale that âyou should let your dog have puppiesâ originated. These days, with millions of unwanted puppies in need of homes, and surgical sterilization being a relatively safe routine procedure, there is no longer any real justification behind the idea that dogs should have a litter.

If you think your dog might have a pyometra, do not delay treatment â the longer you wait, the worse things will get. If you are worried about costs, reach out to local charities or speak to your veterinarian â there may be payment plans or charitable funds available to help.

A dog is never too old to get a pyometra, so even if your dog is considered elderly, unless they have health conditions that make surgery or anesthesia too much of a risk, itâs far better to have them spayed when theyâre healthy rather than risk them getting a pyometra in old age.

Pyometra is a relatively common â and entirely preventable â disease in female dogs. Infection of the uterus can make your dog incredibly sick, and if left untreated, can even be fatal. Signs of pyometra usually appear 2-3 weeks after a season and include increased thirst & urination, lethargy, inappetence, fever, discomfort, and, in the case of an open pyometra, vaginal discharge.

If you suspect your dog may have pyometra, contact your vet immediately â do not delay.

If your dog hasnât been spayed, talk to your vet. Remember, prevention is always better than cure.

#7917. Nick Viall Opens Up About Fatherhood

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

Nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he currently co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

What viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he says. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

How's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

For the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

But it's been really exciting to just be like, "Oh, we already have three kids, and it only took two pregnancies." So easy for me to say, obviously, but it's been really fun.

Well, congratulations. The first question I have is just wondering what kind of dad are you?

I'm a pretty involved dad and pretty hands-on. Natalie and I, ever since we've been together, we just share the responsibilities of our household. And that was true even before we became parents. I was lucky enough to have the parents I had. And I think that the biggest takeaway I had from my childhood is just how my parents worked as a team.

I have 10 brothers and sisters. And my parents were very lower middle class, very blue collar. My mom stayed home and worked. I mean, my mom stayed home and raised the kids, my dad worked, but that wasn't based on some kind of a decision they made. It was more like that was the situation they had.

In terms of the day-to-day, they shared their responsibility. My mom did a lot of the traditional day-to-day keeping up the house, but my dad would often make dinner. My mom sometimes would mow the lawn. It was just more like all hands on deck type of thing, and you just do things as a team. And that's just something Natalie and I implemented into our relationship early on. And then, obviously, when River showed up, it continued. And then Natalie started working with me on the show.

And so really we're just very involved. And so any little thing I can do to help Natalie or just be an involved parent, we're doing things together every step of the way.

So I'm just hyper-involved. There's no her thing, my thing. We conquer and divide, and certainly, we joke where I'm allergic to laundry, she's allergic to dishes. I don't mind doing dishes. She doesn't mind doing laundry. So there's definitely things that we have our preferences, but for the most part, we just share everything.

Nick Viall and Natalie Joy Viall have many joint ventures including, namely, the uber-successful Viall Files relationship advice podcast.

What's one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood or will have?

Well, I feel very fortunate to say that I was lucky enough to try to be able to give the best part of my childhood to my children because I was lucky enough to buy back my grandfather's lake house a couple years ago. And that was a place that in my childhood was like my Nirvana. It was my special place.

Sadly, when my grandfather passed away when I was in the fourth grade, they sold that property, and it was like this devastating moment of my life. It was like some real childhood trauma.

And it was a place that, quite frankly, I had recurring dreams all the way into adulthood. And again, I was lucky enough to buy it back and just really excited that it will be a place that I'll hopefully be able to give to my children, and a place that they'll be able to grow up and we'll have, obviously, a lot of hopefully monumental family events there. So that's definitely something I want them to have.

But thinking in the vein of how times might be different, I think the world's changing so fast. I have such fond memories of going to the movies as a child, going to Blockbuster and picking on a movie and things like that. And some of those moments I hope we'll still be able to do. Or just maybe I hope there's a renaissance of people wanting to get outside, touch grass type of thing. And I hope that's something our children will be able to enjoy.

And certainly, in the lake houses up in the middle of nowhere in Wisconsin will be a great tool to help our kids want to be outside and play in nature and just make-believe. Most of my childhood was a lot of just make believe with my friends outside. And we would ride our bikes all over the place.

It's weird. I'm sure you're probably familiar with that book, The Anxious Generation by Jonathan … he talked about the freedoms that kids used to have back in the day and parents like 5, 10 years ago got a little... it's like you get nervous about the world, but you took for granted, again, the dangers of the phone. And so I'm really hoping my kids get to embrace the world and get outside and play make believe with their friends and things like that. So that's a big focus for us and certainly, hopefully, something that I hope they do get to enjoy because those are always fond memories that I have as a child.

That's a great perspective. I mean, I do agree that right now is a good time to have kids because everyone is much more aware of the difficulties parents are facing . You'll see all the support in elementary school. It's really talked about a lot.

And on to the next question: What does your wife love about you?

Well, I think probably just the fact that, I hope, that I like to think I'm her rock. There's so much burden and pressure on moms postpartum. I like to think that my job is just to be a cheerleader. When I get a sense that she's stressed out or feeling overwhelmed, I'm quick to try to give her a break, tell her to go lie down if that's what she wants to do. I'm always there and always available.

And I hope that's one thing that she loves most about me, but I just try to be as supportive as possible just to remind her and just be a cheerleader. Just always remind her that she's doing a great job because, again, there's just so much pressure that moms put on themselves.

The other side of that coin, what does she maybe find annoying about you?

Oh, my God, the list is so long. Well, I don't know how to close a cupboard. I don't put things away. I leave a trail of destruction wherever I go. I'm messier than our two-year-old. So there is that.

I've recently got back into some video game playing, which definitely gives her the ick, but she is kind enough to let me decompress with a game here or there. So I think she'd prefer it not to exist, but … everything in moderation. Again, the trick for any dad out there who enjoys a video game or two is to never let it get in the way of being helpful. So that's the trick to get it in when you can, but never let it come in the way of, obviously, being a partner and being a father.

What does fatherhood mean to you in the current world?

I mean, it means everything to me. I've had this conversation with a lot of peers that I have, and I have a lot of women friends in the space I work in, and so talked to some new young mothers, young professionals who, obviously, their careers are and still are really important to them.

Once you have a child, I describe it as the easiest North Star. I've been fortunate enough in my life to accomplish a lot of cool things and it's nice to have individual accomplishments and accolades and awards, but they're not always as fulfilling as you think they might be when they happen. Fatherhood, parenthood is just... you always know why you're doing something. You always know what the purpose is. And so even the late nights, it's a drag to get up at 2:00 in the morning, but you know why you're doing it, and you always get a sense of purpose and accomplishment. And it's just the best motivator. No matter what's going on in work or in our personal life, it really calms you down.

I'm a fairly anxious, high-stress guy. It's easy for me to get worried about work and all the things that are going on in this world. And then I have the benefit of coming home, and especially with River now when she greets me. I'm constantly on my phone with work, and I'm never not working in a sense, but when I walk into the house, Natalie's incorporated this kind of best practice of making sure I'm off my phone and I'm very present to greet River. Even if it's for a few minutes, even if I still have some work left to do, I never walk in on the phone and I'm not giving her my undivided attention. And it's something like Natalie incorporated, which I really appreciate that she did, and I think it's just a really great best practice that we do.

Thank you so much for all the thoughtful answers.

I appreciate it, man. It's fun to talk about fatherhood.

It's something I really enjoy. And it's weird because in my... I don't know if you've noticed this. I mean, it's weird how parenting has become, like everything else these days, almost like a polarizing topic. No parent is indifferent about parenting, and obviously, every parent comes with passion, but it's weirdly become a topic that I'd want to talk about more, but sometimes it's like you want to be careful because you don't want to force your thoughts and feelings onto others.

If you're thinking of cleaning your deck with vinegar, take care not to make this mistake...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Somewhere in the pantry there's probably a gallon of white vinegar that already cleans the coffee pot and the shower door. Vinegar costs next to nothing and smells like salad dressing instead of bleach; many people use vinegar to clean a deck for exactly those reasons, without a second thought about where the rinse water goes.

Out in the yard, white vinegar already has a few honest jobs. Some gardeners use vinegar in the garden to scrub crusty clay pots and burn back weeds in sidewalk cracks. That same weed-killing action is part of the problem on a deck, though. Acetic acid burns plant tissue on contact, and a bucket of rinse water doesn't stop at the edge of the boards.

It also matters what the deck is made of. A cedar deck that has never seen a drop of stain, for example? Well, that doesn't play by the same rules as Trex, a major composite brand that actually approves vinegar for one particular job. Check the maker's care guide before any cleaner goes on.

On some composite boards, the answer is a qualified yes. If your boards are one of Trex's current lines, white vinegar is on the approved list for hard water deposits: the chalky white spots a sprinkler leaves when it keeps hitting the same boards.

Rinse well afterward; everyday dirt gets warm soapy water and a soft-bristle brush instead, scrubbed down into the embossed grain. Be aware that Trex says anything containing acid or bleach can lighten the color of its boards, so try a small spot near the steps first.

Other brands say less. TimberTech's care guide doesn't mention vinegar at all, and it points owners toward its own diluted deck cleaner or, for railings, a pH-neutral detergent. It also warns against citrus cleaners, solvents and several brand-name deck cleaners on its current capped boards. When a manufacturer hasn't approved a product, using it anyway means guessing how the surface will react.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Wood decks raise a different question, and the finish on top matters more than the boards underneath. Acids aren't foreign to deck care – oxalic acid brighteners are a standard step for pulling gray discoloration out of bare wood before a fresh coat of stain.

That's prep work for unfinished boards, though; once paint or stain goes on, the can it came in has the final word. Some finish makers approve only their own cleaners, and washing a stained deck with straight vinegar again and again means working outside those directions with no way of knowing how that particular finish will hold up.

Then there's everything growing below the deck rail. Household vinegar is about 5% acetic acid, the same acid sold in stronger form as a weed killer, and it damages leaf tissue wherever it lands.

Picture that rinse water running off the edge of the deck onto a bed of hostas or a row of fall lettuce – leaves that it soaks can turn brown and crispy, and seedlings take the worst of it. The acid doesn't hang around in the soil, and lawn grass along the edge usually recovers better than broadleaf plants do. A natural label? It sadly doesn't change any of that.

The broom comes out first, since scrubbing wet leaves only smears them across the boards. Home Depot's 7-pattern Ames hose nozzle set has a soft shower setting for soaking the deck and a narrow jet for packed gaps. Warm water and a squirt of dish soap handle ordinary grime on wood and composite alike.

Brushes are where the two big composite brands part ways. Trex wants soft bristles, and Home Depot also carries a soft-bristle Unger scrub brush that threads onto a standard broom handle. TimberTech calls for medium-to-stiff nylon on its composite instead. Do one section at a time and rinse it before the suds dry.

Mildew and gray weathering on a wood deck usually need something stronger than soap. Walmart carries DEFY's powdered wood cleaner, an oxygen-based formula for exterior wood that mixes up in a bucket.

Now, at least one stain maker warns that chlorine bleach can damage both the finish and the bare wood fibers, and it's hard on any plants it splashes. Capped composite needs more caution here (TimberTech's guide says its own diluted cleaner is the safe bet). Think about where the bucket water goes, too, especially if the deck slopes toward a fish pond or a storm drain. A label that says biodegradable means the product breaks down eventually, not that it's harmless to fish and other pond life along the way.

Pressure washers are tempting on a big deck, but a narrow stream held too close can tear up the surface of wood boards and leave the fibers fuzzy. Composite brands set firm limits. On Trex Transcend, Enhance and Select boards, the limit is 3,100 psi with a fan tip held at least 8 inches (20.3cm) from the surface, though the company doesn't recommend pressure washers at all on its early-generation lines. TimberTech caps pressure at 1,500 psi, for rinsing only, with the spray running along the grain.

Decks that get washed twice a year are far less likely to need anything harsh. Trex ties its spring and fall schedule to pollen and leaf litter, since that buildup is what mold grows on. Leaves wedged between boards can hold water against the surface long after a rain, and a putty knife slid down the row clears them out quickly. Shady corners and boards under overhanging branches usually go green first.

Keep the vinegar, just not as the everyday deck cleaner. On Trex boards with chalky sprinkler spots, it's the fix the company itself approves, and the potting bench can use it too. Day-to-day grime comes off with warm soapy water and a brush that won't scuff the boards, ideally on a gray afternoon when the sun isn't drying the suds faster than you can scrub.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7915. Thinking About Adopting A Cat? Here Are 4 Things To Ask Before Bringing Them Home

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

This article was created in sponsorship with Mars, which helps make content like this possible.

Pet ownership is booming, but when it comes to adoption, the biggest hurdle isnât willingness; itâs receiving the right support and guidance to adopt with confidence.

Despite there being more than one billion pets worldwide, with cat ownership specifically on the rise, new research from Mars found that 58% of pet owners have not adopted a pet from a shelter or rescue organization. Worries about the unknown, from a petâs health and behavioral history to understanding their nutritional and everyday needs, are just some of the factors that can hold people back from taking that next step.

For prospective cat owners, however, the right preparation and support can make all the difference, especially when nearly a third of respondents globally would consider it with the right support. Mars is #ClearingThePath to pet adoption by giving prospective pet parents practical, expert-backed guidance to navigate the questions that can arise before and after bringing a pet home.

Find out what medical care and health checks the shelter provides as standard. Some initial questions could be what veterinary care your cat has received (if any), including any parasite treatment, which vaccinations they have had, if they are microchipped or neutered, and whether they have any known health concerns or ongoing medications.

Once your cat is home, contact your local veterinarian to establish care for your cat. A check-up soon after adoption can help build a clearer picture of their overall health and create a plan for future preventative care. Itâs a good idea to arrange pet insurance as soon as youâve decided to adopt your cat so theyâre covered for any injuries or illnesses that may arise.

But health is only one part of understanding what your new cat needs to thrive. The SHINEâ¢ framework, developed by the Waltham Petcare Science Institute, looks at five interconnected areas of a petâs wellbeing: socialisation, health, individuality, nutrition and environment.

With that bigger picture in mind, ask the shelter about your catâs personality, temperament, energy levels, previous experiences and interactions with people, children or other pets. Understanding as much as you can about these different needs can help you consider how well your home, family, and daily routine will suit the individual cat, and how you can best support them once they come home.

Mars Research found that 71% of adopters change their petâs diet soon after adoption, but changing food immediately is not usually recommended unless a veterinarian advises it.

Ask the shelter what your cat is currently eating, how often they are fed, and whether they have any special dietary requirements. Your catâs food should be complete and balanced for their life stage, whether they are a kitten, adult, or senior. Keeping their food and feeding routine consistent initially can help make the move feel less disruptive.

If you want to change their food, wait a week or so to allow them to adjust, then do so gradually by adding a small proportion of the new food to their regular diet. On the first day, their old food should make up around three-quarters of the meal, with the new food making up the rest. Gradually increase the proportion of new food each day over a week, giving their digestive system time to get used to the new food.

If you decide to adopt a senior cat (7+ years),â¯diets designed for mature catsâ¯account for the burning of fewer calories throughout the day as well as increased palatability tailored to mature cat preferences.

Importantly, cats need diets that provide appropriate protein and essential nutrients, along with constant access to fresh water. Portion size, nutrition, and feeding style should reflect your catâs activity, age, body condition, and health; treats should remain below 10% of daily calories.

A veterinarian can help choose the most suitable diet if your cat has medical or weight concerns.

Although it can be tempting to let your new feline friend explore everywhere straight away, for many cats, a smaller and more predictable environment can feel much safer.

Consider keeping your new cat in one room before slowly giving them access to the rest of the home. During the first few days, keep windows secured and doors closed, and make sure they have everything they need close by.

Cats will seek out hiding spaces when they feel stressed, so itâs important to provide some quiet resting places while they settle in. Providing safe places to retreat to will help them navigate the unfamiliar sights, sounds, and smells around them.

Something as simple as a cardboard box placed on its side or an open cat carrier can offer a reassuring place to hide, giving them confidence to explore and interact.

Many pets need time to adjust to being alone in a new home. Start by gradually introducing short periods of separation and pairing alone time with positive experiences, such as treats, toys, or enrichment activities. Keeping departures and arrivals calm and predictable can also help build confidence and reduce stress.

If your pet shows signs of significant separation anxiety, such as destructive behavior, excessive vocalization, or distress when left alone, speak with your veterinarian or a qualified behavior professional for support and guidance.

#7914. Charles M. Schulz Museum With Kids: A Family Guide To Santa Rosa, CA

Between the Charles M. Schulz Museum, a play-forward children’s museum, and dessert-first dinners, this Sonoma County town is basically Charlie Brown’s world IRL.

When the chance came to visit Santa Rosa, California, and experience the Charles M. Schulz Museum, the timing couldn’t have been more perfect. Our little one is ~deep~ in a Snoopy phase. We’ve been rotating Peanuts classics with The Snoopy Show on Apple TV+ because they’re such great low-stimulation wind-down shows before bed (parents included). So Peanuts Gang vibes were definitely what we wanted out of a family trip, and Santa Rosa delivered: walkable cozy dining, cute cartoon sightings around every corner, and plenty for a little kid to get into.

Getting there was definitely the most stressful part because our once-dozing darling of the skies had grown into a ball of energy bouncing around the cabin. Thankfully, the flight was only an hour long from our home base of Los Angeles. Once we hit the road the rest of the way in a rental car, our drive from San Francisco to Santa Rosa washed away the stress as we road-tripped over the water on the Golden Gate Bridge and into the lush greenery of Sonoma County. Visit Santa Rosa hosted Scary Mommy at the Art House Hotel and put together a family-friendly itinerary built around the Charles M. Schulz Museum and the Children’s Museum of Sonoma County, with some of the town’s best food mixed in.

First up was the Poppy Bank Epicenter, where we got to shake loose energy from all the travel sitting. There’s a toddler play area, an arcade, bowling, and Sky Zone, where if your kid is too restless to sit for food, you can pack it up and head over to an activity to tire them out. Ask us how we know. We’re in the restaurant training era, and she was just not having it. Still, Victory House at Epicenter was a great spot; we got massive burgers with fries, plus kids' dino nuggets to go. After a workout on the awesome 4-person Omni Motion VR screen games, we headed back to the hotel to put her to bed and reheat our food.

Here's where Art House really shines for families. Once our little one knocked out, we were able to make use of a full kitchen and sit down at a real dining table to eat like actual adults while still keeping an eye on our snoozing kid. Have you ever eaten cold pizza on a hotel bed in the dark because the baby finally fell asleep? Yeah, then you get why this felt like such a luxury.

The next morning, my husband picked up coffee from Land and Water Coffee, a local roaster with flavorful and sense-awakening brews. It gave us the energy we needed to keep up with our kid, who was raring to go. Our breakfast spot was the Americana, a farm-to-table breakfast nook where we filled up on fresh veggie-packed, cheesy omelets and our daughter happily demolished chocolate chip pancakes with chicken sausage and a milk.

Everything was either walkable or just a short drive away, which meant we could really plan around our kid’s schedule instead of the other way around. Our first big outing of the trip was to The Children’s Museum of Sonoma County, just steps from the Schulz Museum (on the deck for the next day). And it just so happened to be her first-ever children’s museum, so we were just as excited for our precocious kid.

Established by a group of mothers in Sonoma, including Lucasfilm luminaries, the children’s museum grew from a traveling trailer of imaginative play and education into a permanent nonprofit space focused on making fun accessible to local families regardless of income. There’s an admission fee, but families who qualify, including WIC and SNAP recipients, can have it waived through the museum’s family access programs.

The level of love and diversity in every experience was so deeply moving. We started my kid in Totopia, a soft-play woodland nook, because we were nervous to let her roam right away. The staff there were great — not just with her, but with us too, gently coaching Mom and Dad to a place where our anxiety could subside. And with so many safe spaces built for creative play, it didn’t take long for all of us to relax.

Next up was the Wild Zone, a purposeful recreational area full of sticks, climbing, and wobbly unstructured natural play where kids can basically FAFO under supervision. So if they lose their balance by maybe climbing something too ambitiously, they learn consequences. Our kiddo needed that lesson! An experimental FAFO space? Genius, truly.

Outside, our daughter fell hard for the bubble and water tables, because what toddler doesn’t yearn for splish-splashing? Take it from us: You’ll want to pack a change of clothes, because we definitely had to change her before going inside. Back indoors, she “flew” a rocket to space, “cooked” in a retro diner, and “doctored” in the Science & Medical Lab. Then it was back to the hotel for naps all around before heading out on foot to our next family adventure.

Our final day in Santa Rosa brought us to the main event: the Snoopy and Family exhibit at the Charles M. Schulz Museum. Since we had a flight to catch later that day, we swung in for sandwiches at Mac’s Deli (they’re legendary for a reason) and coffee from Espressioso's Coffee, a Latin-inspired roaster specializing in ethically sourced beans.

After getting in a little playtime in the cafe's toddler corner, we made our way to the museum. As animation fans, we geeked out seeing the comic strips up close and learning the story behind Snoopy’s litter of siblings, the focus of the current exhibit. We especially appreciated that it spotlights Bill Melendez, the director and animator behind the Peanuts TV specials — including the one about Snoopy’s origin — as such an integral part of making Peanuts a staple in pop culture.

It was so cool to see how those relatable Snoopy family moments came to life, from being printed on local paper strips by Schulz to the screen by Melendez. In particular, the "Snoopy's Reunion” episode really captures the spirit of Schulz’s work, and how Snoopy’s backstory only made fans love him more. I didn’t know much about Melendez before this visit (including that the Latino animator was the voice of Snoopy himself), and learning about his mark on animation history genuinely moved me. He and Schulz created a vision of childhood still beloved today.

Now I get to share that with my daughter, who is fully in her cartoon dog era. She was surrounded by puppies everywhere she looked, and the giant plush displays of Snoopy with Spike, Belle, Olaf, and the rest of the Daisy Hill Puppy Farm litter gave me full-blown cuteness aggression. Thankfully, there’s a gift shop stocked with Peanuts merch from around the world.

The museum also has art rooms where you can sit down and draw the Peanuts gang, which our daughter loved. Special tables let you trace classic strips and put your own spin on them; I made one to commemorate my little one’s first visit. We also hammed it up in the photo-op installations, including (yes!) Lucy’s psychiatry booth. Nearby, there’s an ice rink where you can skate just like the gang, plus The Warm Puppy Cafe, a Snoopy-themed comfort-food spot serving pot pies, pizza, chili, and hot cocoa.

The whole trip had the gentle, unhurried pace of an idyllic visit to Charlie Brown’s world. All that was missing was a jazz score by the show’s iconic theme composer, Vince Guaraldi! It was lovely to dig into the history of Peanuts and its timeless take on childhood, which Santa Rosa holds onto with such a charming specificity. We’re already plotting a return trip to see if the Great Pumpkin shows up in the fall, or to catch some Charlie Brown Christmas magic.

#7913. Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

It’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

But authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

What Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

You say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

She doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

What kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A big part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

So you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

No. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.

There was a time when any tree injury had us reaching for cans of black tar and wound dressings, but is sealing really a good idea? Here’s the truth about what your trees need

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some garden wisdom isn’t really wise at all. Have you ever heard that sprinkling used coffee grounds around hydrangeas adds oodles of acid to the soil, or that peony buds won’t open unless ants tickle their petals? Far from being wisdoms, these are classic examples of garden folklore: ideas that have been repeated so often across fences and forums that people simply assume they are true.

Welcome back to Garden Mythbusters, where we aim to separate fact from fiction with persistent gardening beliefs. We have already examined whether gravel at the bottom of pots truly helps drainage and the idea that bulbs need to be planted pointy side up. Here’s another one that you might not even have suspected was a myth: the idea that when you sever a branch or clean up storm damage, you must slather the fresh wood with pruning paint or tar sealant to prevent rot, pests, and disease.

For generations, we’ve been encouraged to buy sealants and dressings to protect our damaged trees. Watching an oak or maple bleed sap feels alarming, and reaching for a sealant seems like a responsible way to shield against infection. But should you really seal a tree wound? Indeed, could slathering a cut with wound dressing be doing more harm than good? It seems true tree recovery requires a much simpler approach. Let’s set the record straight once and for all…

To understand why tree wound sealants became a thing in the first place, there’s a simple (and admittedly silly) explanation. We are prone to anthropomorphism, which means that we think all life forms are prone to reacting like us. So we project our own biological experiences onto plants and wildlife. People once imagined tree wounds needed sealing because they assumed that trees heal like humans, basically.

When a person suffers a deep scrape or laceration, the protocol is clear: clean the cut, stop the bleeding, apply antiseptic ointment, and seal the opening to block external pathogens while our cells heal. Gardeners back in the day figured trees would also need a protective Band-Aid to keep tree sap in and bugs and disease out. When a heavy limb snapped in a summer gale or was lopped off during seasonal pruning, the exposed heartwood looked vulnerable, and any sap seemed alarming.

Gardeners made the mistake of thinking that if they left this tree damage exposed to the elements, wood-boring beetles could march right in, airborne fungal spores might colonize the moist sapwood, and the tree would might bleed to death. By the early 20th century, several petroleum-based asphalt paints, chemical tar compounds, and thick sealants were marketed as miracle aids for healing. The problem? Beneath those seemingly protective layers, the reality was far from protective.

It wasn't until the late 20th century that arborists and tree scientists found that routine sealants can cause more harm than good. They ran rigorous, controlled trials on tree wound dressings and they found that painting tree wounds does not prevent decay or add protection. In study after study, sealed wounds rotted faster and suffered more internal structural breakdown than wounds left exposed to the open air.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Today, leading forestry institutions and the International Society of Arboriculture (ISA) advise against the routine application of wound paints and sealants. The core problem is that wound dressings alter the microclimate of the cut surface. Asphalt paints and sealants dry into an imperfect crust. As the tree barks expand and contracts in shifting weather and humidity, the paint hairline-cracks. Rainwater seeps into these tiny fissures, but the sealant prevents that moisture from evaporating.

When you apply sealant on a tree wound, it traps water inside the wound, allowing bacteria to thrive and fungi to cause decay. The sealant also impedes the tree’s natural healing process. Thick dressings physically smother living plant cells along wound margins, impairing the tree's ability to produce vital callus tissue. By attempting to protect the wound, growers may seal pathogens inside the tree, while locking out the fresh air that recovery demands.

That’s not to say you can’t help out a stressed tree. There are amendments you can add at the ground level to help tree roots with the process of recovery. For example, a light sprinkling of mycorrhizal fungi can assist with rejuvenation. You can buy PureMyco Mycorrhizal Fungi Root Inoculant from Amazon to encourage root growth in stressed trees. But in terms of the trunk or branch, the general opinion now is that clean, unsealed tree cuts heal best on their own.

It’s rare to find a general rule without exceptions. This new expert opinion that sealant should not be used for most tree wounds also has a few exceptions. There are a couple of scientifically backed occasions where dressings can be an essential defense. These exceptions do not exist to help the tree heal faster. Rather, they serve as a barrier to protect specific species against insect-borne epidemics.

The primary time when you might use a sealant safely involves native oak species and elms. In regions where oak wilt or Dutch elm disease are prevalent, fresh pruning cuts or storm tears can result in a leaking sap that attracts beetles that spread deadly diseases like oak wilt and Dutch elm disease. If an oak or elm suffers accidental storm breakage or requires emergency trimming during the high-risk growing season (spring through mid-summer), It’s wise to apply a very thin layer of plain, water-based latex paint or specialized tree wound spray over the cut surface.

A safe sealant option in this case is Tanglefoot Tree Sealant Aerosol, available from Walmart, which is beneficial for emergency summer cuts on oak and elm. The goal is to mask the scent of sap from foraging beetles. Once outside this active insect window, even oaks and elms should be pruned cleanly and left unpainted.

To understand why artificial sealants are generally unnecessary, just bear in mind that trees do not heal like animals do. Trees don’t have the same circulatory system that humans do. Human wounds need closing to prevent loss of bloom, but trees don’t have these issues. Instead, when you prune a tree, the tree initiates a process called tree compartmentalization.

Research led by USDA Forest Service plant pathologist Dr Alex Shigo revealed that trees cannot replace or regenerate damaged heartwood. Instead, they build walls to seal off injured tissue from the rest of the tree. This is called compartmentalization of decay in trees (CODIT). The moment a branch is severed, the tree activates an internal defense consisting of multiple boundaries. Simultaneously, the outer edges of the wound produce swollen ridges of tissue known as callus wood.

Trees start compartmentalizing as soon as you prune them. Cells near the cut area form a cork layer between the wound and the healthy wood inside. Cork is dense and moisture-resistant and quickly forms a natural dressing. At the same time as the tree starts building a callus around the wound, the edge of the cut starts making healthy tissue. This new wood starts growing on the outside, but continues inward until the entire cut surface is covered. This can take years, but ultimately the wound is overgrown. And it works best if you leave the cut alone and let the tree manage it.

Because trees rely on specialized anatomical structures to build their natural defense walls, your pruning technique matters far more than anything that comes out of a can. Proper cuts empower the tree’s natural CODIT defense system, while improper cuts compromise its defenses. Make sure you always use sharp, sterilized pruners or saws. The sharper the blades, the cleaner the cuts. If you need a hand saw, the Fiskars 10-Inch Folding Soft Grip Handsaw, available from Walmart, gives a good grip when cutting through thicker tree branches.

Always cut outside the branch collar when pruning. Look for the junction where a limb meets the parent branch or trunk. The swollen shoulder of textured wood is the branch collar. This collar is packed with cells hardwired to generate those CODIT barrier walls. Make your cut just outside this swollen collar. Never make a flush cut against the trunk, as slicing into the collar invites trunk rot. Don’t leave a 6-inch (15cm) dead branch protruding from the trunk, either, as this is also damaging. The tree cannot compartmentalize dead tissue inches away from the collar.

Large branches are heavy and prone to tearing the trunk if cut from the top. To prevent this, first make a shallow upward cut on the underside of the limb, about 12 inches (30cm) from the trunk. Cut one-third of the way through. Then from above, cut through the limb from the other direction, 2-3 inches (5-8cm) out from the first cut. The branch should break cleanly between the cuts without tearing bark. Finally, make a single, clean cut just outside the branch collar to remove the stub. Once you’re done, leave the cut bare and allow the fresh wood to dry and air-heal.

Storms can rip major limbs from trees, leaving jagged stumps and stripped bark. The secret to storm recovery is acting quickly to clean up jagged breaks so those natural compartmentalization mechanisms can engage. First, never approach trees that are tangled in utility lines or have hanging widow-maker branches suspended overhead. Call professional utility crews or an ISA-certified arborist for high-canopy work.

Always wear safety equipment like a hard hat, safety glasses and sturdy gloves. And avoid uprooted trees or split trunks. They could shift in the wind and fall. After that, assess the damage and determine what can be saved. Wind often twists branches off, tearing strips of living bark down the trunk. Using a sharp utility knife or hand chisel, trim away any loose, jagged flaps of bark, creating a smooth, clean margin around the wound. Keep the healthy inner cambium intact.

Jagged, splintered branch stumps cannot seal properly. Trace the shattered limb back to the nearest healthy branch union or just outside the branch collar, and make a clean, flat saw cut. If a storm strips more than 50% of a tree's canopy, or if the main trunk has split down the center, structural recovery is unlikely. However, if more than half of the canopy remains intact, the tree possesses sufficient power to compartmentalize the damage and rebuild its crown over several seasons.

Pruned or storm-stressed trees need moisture rather than fertilizer. Apply a 2-3-inch (5-8cm) layer of organic wood mulch over the roots, keeping it 6 inches (15cm) away from the trunk flare. Our team favorite is Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help regulate ground conditions and retain moisture to support damaged trees.

It can be difficult to resist the urge to bandage a damaged tree, especially when a favorite suffers a traumatic break. But these tree-loving insights can hopefully give you the confidence to step back a bit and let Mother Nature lend a helping hand. Trees are ancient, resilient entities, equipped with extraordinary internal defense mechanisms that have preserved them beautifully for many, many years. So skip artificial wound dressings and focus on making precise cuts outside the branch collar, smoothing ragged storm tears, and supporting root health with mulch and consistent hydration, and you’ll give your trees the ability to heal themselves.

#7911. The Time Change Wrecks My Entire Family Every Single Year

Apparently, moving the clock one hour is enough to bring our whole household to its knees.

Every year, someone cheerfully announces that daylight saving time is ending as if we have all just won an extra hour of sleep. And every year, I wonder who exactly is receiving this free hour, because it is certainly not the parents.

In my house, the time change does not feel like gaining an hour. It feels like someone picked up our entire routine, shook it like an Etch A Sketch, and handed it back with a smile.

Dinner is suddenly happening at the wrong time. Bedtime feels suspicious. Morning arrives before anyone’s brain has agreed to participate. By 5:30 p.m., it’s pitch-black outside and my body is convinced we have missed bedtime by at least three business days.

People tend to talk about the time change as a problem for parents of babies and toddlers. There are entire survival guides devoted to shifting naps by 15-minute increments so a two-year-old does not greet the day at 4:12 a.m.

But once your child gets older, everyone seems to assume the problem disappears. It does not disappear. The child just gets taller and develops stronger opinions about why bedtime is a government conspiracy.

My son is 11 now. He is not a toddler. He can read a clock. He understands, intellectually, that we moved it back one hour. None of that means his body, brain, appetite, attention span, or emotional regulation received the memo.

The clock may say 7:00, but his nervous system is operating in its own private time zone… and frankly, so is mine.

That is the part I think we miss when we talk about older kids and daylight saving time. We treat it like a scheduling inconvenience instead of what it really is for some families: a disruption to the external cues that help our brains know what comes next.

My son may be old enough to understand what happened, but understanding is not the same as adjusting. Older kids still have circadian rhythms. They still rely on environmental cues. ADHD does not pack its bags and leave just because a child can make his own sandwich. Anxiety does not check the calendar and decide middle schoolers are too mature to be affected by sleep disruption.

And, for the record, adults are not magically immune either. I am 42 years old, and the time change absolutely wrecks me. It takes one dark afternoon for my motivation to crawl into a cave. Suddenly, I am tired at 6:00 p.m., wide awake when I should be sleeping, and personally offended by the sun for abandoning us before dinner.

My brain already has a complicated relationship with time. Moving every clock in the house and changing when daylight appears is not the tiny administrative update society pretends it is.

Meanwhile, life does not pause for adjustment. School still starts at the same number on the clock. Homework still needs to happen. Dinner still needs to materialize through the ancient magic of a mother staring into the refrigerator and hoping the ingredients will organize themselves.

Everyone is more tired, less patient, and somehow surprised that the evening is not going smoothly.

This is usually when parents start blaming themselves.

We think the routine is failing because we have become inconsistent. We wonder why our older child is suddenly moodier, more impulsive, harder to wake, or completely done with humanity by late afternoon. We tell ourselves they should be able to handle a one-hour change.

But one hour is not always just one hour. It is darkness arriving before our brains expect it. It is hunger, attention, sleep, and transitions all showing up slightly out of order. It is the fragile after-school window getting even narrower. It is a child holding it together through seven hours of school and arriving home with absolutely nothing left in the emotional gas tank. It is a neurodivergent parent trying to regulate a neurodivergent child while her own nervous system is also filing a formal complaint.

So this year, I am lowering the bar before the clocks even change. For a few days, dinner can be embarrassingly easy. Bedtime may need to start earlier, even if my middle schooler insists he is basically an adult. Mornings may require more alarms, more light, and fewer unnecessary conversations.

If homework feels harder, emotions run hotter, or we are both staring blankly at each other by 7:00 p.m., I am going to remember that our bodies are adjusting instead of deciding we have suddenly lost every coping skill we ever learned.

I am also refusing to romanticize the whole thing.

Yes, fall is beautiful. Yes, the leaves are gorgeous. Yes, cozy evenings sound lovely in theory. But there is nothing cozy about being trapped in a dark house at 5:45 p.m. with a dysregulated child, an untouched homework assignment, and the dawning realization that bedtime is still hours away.

So if your entire household becomes a little feral when the clocks change, you are not imagining it… and you are not failing.

Keep the routines you can. Add more light, more rest, and more grace where you can find them. Feed everyone something requiring the fewest possible dishes. Give the family a little time to recalibrate.

The clock only moved an hour. Unfortunately, no one told our nervous systems it was supposed to be no big deal.

Danielle Kelly is the host of the ADHD parenting podcast Chaos & Caffeine, which reaches thousands of families each month and was recently named one of the Best Kids With ADHD Podcasts of 2026 by PodRanker.

#7908. “I’m Glad I’m The Default Parent” & 49 Other Anonymous Mom Confessions

Seasonal depression, is that you creeping in? Because, fair warning, this week’s confessions are heavy. Sure, we usually have some tough stuff sandwiched between crushes and spicy feelings and your garden-variety MIL woes. But something is shifting, and it seems as though maybe it’s shifting right as our clocks are shifting, too.

And maybe there is something to that. After all, women experience seasonal affective disorder (a type of depression that follows a seasonal pattern) at roughly four times the rate men do. Cool, cool, cool... another thing to add to the list. Oh, and need we mention that mercury is also currently in retrograde?!

Then again, moms are feelers. It’s in our nature. And maybe we’re just feeling the weight of the world on our shoulders even more lately since, well, it’s extra weighty right now. So it’s no surprise that a lot of what moms had to say this week had to do with being at max capacity. Some moms want to rewind to their carefree pre-kid years. Lots are considering leaving their partners. Many just want one day where nobody needs anything from them.

Don’t worry; it’s not all worry and dread. One mom is having the best sex of her life in her 50s (get it, sis). A few are celebrating major milestones.

But whatever’s weighing on you at the moment, just know that somebody in this list has confessed some version of it. Here are this week’s confessions, shared anonymously by moms who clearly needed to lighten their load.

Scary Mommy Confessions are a tried-and-true part of what makes our site so fun. If you want to anonymously confess, look for our weekly callouts on Instagram. And to browse past Confessions, take a look here.

My husband is having the best sex of his life with me. I, on the other hand, am not.

I’ve gone from Needoh hunting to estrogen patch hunting 🙈

I wish I could start my life over and make different choices.

I’m worried my husband is ruining his relationship with our son. They hate each other.

Should I take the leap and become a solo mother by choice? I’m scared.

Still living with my ex and it’s starting to feel weird. I want to leave, but I can’t afford it.

Going through a friend breakup and feeling more relieved than sad. Not everyone is forever.

The long drought is over! 2yrs, 11mos, 2wks & 3 days. Been with my partner 17 years 😤

Our dog passed away and it hurts worse than losing prior family members.

My mom died two years ago this week, and I can’t handle this time of year still so I drink wine.

I never get a break as a single mom and I’m so tired.

Going through perimenopause and my sex drive is much higher than my husband’s. I feel ashamed!

My daughter is overweight like I was and I feel like the world is against her too.

I wish my son’s father would just stop trying to pretend to parent; he’s causing our son anxiety.

I miss something I never had with someone I couldn’t have. I loved him. He didn’t love me.

I really have lost hope that there is romantic love for me out there.

Just once I’d like to come home to the smell of food cooking without me having to plan it.

I can’t afford the holidays this year and idk what to do since they all still believe in Santa.

My husband’s drinking is obnoxious. It’s so unattractive and he is so handsome.

Blasting music in the car when I’m alone just to feel myself again. Even if it’s just for a moment.

If I could go back to my younger self, I’d tell her not to get married. I’m so over parenting a grown man.

I want to run away from my whole life and be a teenager again.

Life would be easier if I could divorce my husband. I do everything on my own anyway.

I fear my mom is racist as heck and I am embarrassed.

I’m tired of the hard. When is it my turn for good things?

My husband had an affair, and there was a silver lining. We are now more connected than ever.

I can’t wait for this election to be over.

I love spending time with my daughter. I’m sad when she is doing her own thing!

Advocating for my neurodivergent child is exhausting.

I have a 10-year-old girl who is completely in puberty, and she treats me like garbage.

I’m angry that it took almost nine months of medical visits to get my shoulder treated.

I lost 20 pounds in the last two months, and no one has noticed or acknowledged it.

Scared for my hysterectomy and entering menopause at 39.

I’m working hard on cutting out alcohol. I’m done with it taking up so much space.

I’m in my late 50s and having the best sex of my life!

I wish my adult children would get their own lives.

Today was the first day back to school after a school shooting and I’m so sad for our community.

I keep having to ask my husband for affection. I can’t remember the last time he gave me a big hug.

I miss the days pre-kids when I lived in an apartment alone and could do cereal for dinner.

Before the recycling goes out, pull a few things aside. Cardboard boxes, old sheets, milk jugs, and more can carry plants through a light frost for free.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Frost warnings in October can seem to arrive with barely a day's notice. One evening, the forecast dips toward freezing while the peppers are still loaded and the fall lettuce is finally filling out. Good frost protection on a night like that doesn't have to come from a garden center.

Before buying frost cloth, take a look in the recycling bin. Last week's delivery boxes, milk jugs, and newspapers can protect plants from frost for a night or two, and the old bedsheet in the linen closet will cover a whole bed of peppers.

There's a limit to what cardboard and cotton can do. They'll carry plants through a light frost, the kind that whitens the lawn at dawn and is gone by mid-morning, but not a freeze that sits in for days. First frosts are often followed by weeks of mild weather, though, and getting tender crops past that one night can stretch the harvest.

So why does a thin bedsheet make any difference? On a clear, calm night, the soil gives off the heat it soaked up during the day, and with no clouds overhead, that warmth drifts up and away. Covers catch some of it on the way out. Drape yours loosely so the edges reach the ground, and the stems have some air space – Home Depot sells steel grow tunnel hoops with a row cover for lifting fabric over a whole garden bed.

Once the air warms above freezing in the morning, the covers need to come off, or they'll trap heat and moisture around the plant. Plastic is the riskiest material here. Wherever it presses against leaves, it carries the cold straight through, so it belongs on a frame or over a fabric layer, never directly on foliage. An analog outdoor thermometer, like this one from Walmart, hung near the garden, makes the morning check easier, though air at ground level can run a few degrees colder on still nights.

Stash these as they come through the house, and keep them dry until a frost advisory goes out.

Flip a box over the plant at dusk. If the cardboard presses on the tips of a young shrub or pepper plant, go up a size and fold the flaps inward so the edges rest on the soil. Container herbs can go under one too. Set a brick on top if there's any wind in the forecast, since an empty box weighs next to nothing. Cardboard also blocks every bit of light and turns soft in heavy dew. It needs to come off first thing in the morning.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

A queen-size flat sheet will stretch over a good length of border. Save pillowcases for the odd small plant. By morning, a cotton sheet is often heavy with dew, and stakes or tomato cages pushed into the bed first keep that weight off tender stems. Rocks along the hem will hold it, or you can snap a few row cover clamps from Home Depot onto the stakes. A tarp over the top helps on rainy nights, as long as none of that plastic touches leaves.

Cut the bottom off a gallon (3.8L) milk jug, and it becomes a mini cloche for a seedling or a young head of lettuce. That's the same idea behind the reusable plastic cloche from Walmart, though a rinsed jug costs nothing. Press the open edge an inch or so (2.5cm) into the soil to keep it from blowing over, and leave the cap on for cold nights. Twist the cap off on sunny days to let heat escape – a sealed jug in full sun warms up fast.

On a frosty night, the roots in a patio pot sit only a pot wall away from the cold air, while roots in the ground have soil all around them. Bubble wrap taped around the outside of the pot, below the rim, gives them a layer of trapped air to slow heat loss. Since the wrap never touches the plant, it can stay on through a stretch of cold weather, and pots pushed together against a sheltered wall hold their warmth a little better.

If you can't save up enough bubble wrap for your plants, then it's worth picking up a roll of Amazon Basics bubble wrap.

If there's newspaper around the house, spread a few sections several layers thick over low, tender plants and young vegetables, or roll one sheet into a cone for a single seedling. Weigh the corners with rocks or a scoop of soil. Once the dew soaks in, paper loses much of its insulating value. Take it off in the morning and let it dry. On wetter nights, a polypropylene frost blanket, like this one from Home Depot, holds up better.

Rake the leaves into a pile and leave them there for now. Once the soil has cooled in late fall, a few inches heaped around a tender perennial will insulate its crown and roots, though they won't help the foliage. Spread too early, and a leaf layer keeps the ground warm and can give voles a spot to settle in. Shred the leaves with a mower first or a leaf mulcher, like this Worx one from Amazon – the pieces stay loose and drain well – and leave a small gap around each stem so the crown doesn't sit wet all winter.

Slide a whole toilet paper tube, or a third of a paper towel tube, over a seedling or young transplant and push it about an inch (2.5cm) into the soil. That little collar stops cutworms such as the black cutworm (Agrotis ipsilon) from chewing through the stem at the soil line, and it takes some of the bite out of a cold wind, too. Tubes won't do much against frost by themselves, though, so pair them with a milk jug or newspaper on cold nights.

Boxes in the garage and old sheets in the closet can carry a garden through those first chilly nights. Pull the covers each morning, fold them up, and they'll be ready the next time the forecast drops. With a little luck, a few more peppers will ripen before the season wraps up.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
