#7906. 17 Easy Holiday Cocktail Recipes That'll Make You Feel Merry & Bright

Whether you’re hosting a holiday party or just want to sip on a special beverage alone by the fire, now is the time when much of the world goes searching for easy holiday cocktail recipes. We all deserve a little treat after the year that was 2025. Well, rest assured, there’s a fun and festive drink out there for every palate (including if mocktails are more your speed). From spiked hot chocolate and eggnog concoctions for sweets lovers to wintry old-fashioneds and martinis, here are some of the best easy holiday cocktails on the internet.

If you’ve never put Bailey’s in your eggnog, now’s the time. Averie Cooks’ recipe for Santa’s magic potion will help you get the ratio just right, and hit it with a little cinnamon and nutmeg for that perfect holiday flavor.

Mimosas are a crowd-pleasing cocktail, so why not just put a holiday spin on them for your winter party? Damn Delicious’ cranberry mimosas blend orange, pineapple, and cranberry juice with sparkling white wine. Just top with a sprig of rosemary and a couple cranberries and serve.

If you’re not a bourbon fan, might I recommend Princess Pinky Girl’s drunken Rudolph, a hot chocolate cocktail spiked with Fireball instead? This recipe is even less work and is sort of the everyman’s version, if you will.

Family Fresh Meals’ starry night punch recipe is nonalcoholic, but obviously you can just swap the sparkling grape juice for the real thing. It will yield a classic Christmas red sangria, which you can top with star-shaped apple cutouts for the perfect finishing touch.

If you want a cocktail that absolutely screams Christmas, then Dude That Cookz’ peppermint cream martini is the drink for you. It’s a delicious mix of peppermint schnapps, white cream liqueur, and vanilla vodka, with the cutest crushed-candy-cane rim.

Why haven’t I thought of apple cider sangria before? Averie Cooks explains everything you’ll need and how to get the perfect balance of flavors. Then just load ‘er up with apples, cinnamon sticks, oranges, pomegranate, and whatever else your holiday heart desires.

Personally, I swore off blue drinks after one particularly rough hangover in college, but Princess Pinky Girl’s Jack Frost cocktail is admittedly very fun-looking. Just blend your ingredients together, rim your glass, and clink it with a friend’s.

One last mimosa idea before you go, courtesy of Budget Bytes: simply swap out orange juice for apple cider, pour it into your champagne flute until the color is just right, and bada bing bada boom. It doesn’t get any easier than that, and you know it’s going to be delish.

Oh, so you’re having a holiday party party — love that. Then you have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s Instagram-worthy candy cane shots, which only take about five minutes to whip up. Adding a little sweetened condensed milk to the gelatin mix gives it a sweet, creamy base that makes the candy cane flavor really come alive.

Biscuits & Burlap’s spiced pear and chai bourbon drink is the perfect reminder that apples are not the only seasonal fruit worth celebrating. It’s a bit more involved (you’ll need to make a fresh pear simple syrup), but the end result looks so worth that little bit of time and effort.

Speaking of pears, you’ve gotta try Dinners Done Quick’s pear gin fizz. When’s the last time you actually ordered a gin fizz out? They’re so good but they’re never really on cocktail menus anymore, and they give me an old-timey celebratory feel every time.

Moscow mules are the perfect drink to serve to guests if you’re not much of a bartender and you’re just out here doing your best as a host. Fresh Apron’s recipe is a matter of a few simple steps (complete with exact measurements); it’s the festive garnishes and copper mugs that really make this beverage shine.

Savory Spice’s recipe will teach you how to make a chai simple syrup (very useful if you’re an at-home coffee enthusiast, by the way) and how to balance it perfectly within a cranberry fizz. It’ll add a seasonal, cozy depth of flavor that’s unexpected yet oddly perfect.

White russian drinkers, you’ll love this easy apple pie cocktail, made with Crown and RumChata, from Dinners Done Quick. You can easily customize it to make it sweeter, heavier on the cinnamon, extra apple-y, however you take your cocktails.

Be honest: How many gallons of apple cider did you just add to your grocery list?

As the growing season winds down, some plants benefit from a final tidy-up. But knowing what to cut – and what to leave alone – is crucial.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While the cold weather and dropped leaves of November make it seem as if the gardening season is over, there’s still one task left: pruning. Certain plants benefit from a pre-winter trim, while others shouldn’t be touched with pruners until next year.

Some perennials should be cut back all the way right now, while other types of plants, like fruiting vines and certain shrubs, can be touched up more lightly. Exact timing for these tasks depends on your location, weather, and the plant.

Here, we’ll outline some late fall pruning basics and list some of the plants you can tidy up or trim back now, before winter fully takes hold. We also share which plants are better trimmed next season.

Peonies are notoriously susceptible to fungal diseases. The deciduous foliage will die back in fall and, if left in place, can allow fungal spores to overwinter and reinfect plants next year. Trim back foliage once the leaves have yellowed or browned, or earlier if they look diseased.

November is the right time for this chore in many places, but if you garden in a warmer climate, the timing might be later. Remove all of the foliage without cutting it too close to the plant’s crown.

Another herbaceous perennial common in many gardens, hostas die back in fall. Clearing away the spent foliage tidies up beds, makes spring cleaning easier, and prevents many pests and diseases from overwintering and spreading. Cut leaves back to the base without getting too close to or cutting into the crowns. As long as leaves are still green, keep them in place to collect energy. Wait until they die back.

Gardeners are often tempted to cut back the leaves of these early bloomers soon after flowering, but it’s important to wait. The green leaves continue collecting energy to store for next year’s flowers. As long as they are healthy, keep the leaves in place until they start dying back in fall. November is a typical time for pruning bearded irises in many gardens. Cut the fans back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As with irises, you don’t want to trim back leaves just because the plants have finished flowering. Let healthy, green leaves stay in place to gather energy. For many gardeners, daylily leaves will be ready to cut back by November. In warmer climates, you might not trim them back until December. Cut daylily leaves back to a few inches above the ground.

Summer-fruiting raspberries develop fruit on canes that are two years old. Once they’re done fruiting, these older canes use up energy that the plant could be using on new canes and next year’s fruit. Identify the older, woodier canes that fruited this year, and trim them back to the ground.

You’ll also see newer, greener canes. Do not cut these back, or you’ll lose next year’s berries. Tie them together or to a support, like a fence, to protect them from winter winds.

Grapevines need regular pruning to maintain their size and structure and to support abundant fruit production. Timing is important. The vines should be dormant, so they don’t lose too much sap or sprout fresh growth. You also don’t want to prune too late, after hard freezes turn vines too brittle to make clean cuts.

When you find the right time to prune your grapevines, remove dead, damaged, or poorly positioned vines and canes. Identify healthy, young vines and trim around these. Don’t remove all older wood, especially the main trunk and arms.

Lavender hedges that are cold-hardy, like English lavender, benefit from a late fall or early winter trim to maintain their shape and health and protect them from winter weather. Too much material left on the plants can accumulate snow and ice that damage the crowns. Trim these lavenders back by about a third before the real freezing weather begins.

Pro gardeners can't get enough of Felco pruners – and these scored top in our testing.

This handy sharpener keeps pruners in top condition for clean cuts.

This telescopic tool is brilliant for trimming trees and tall climbers – no ladders required.

While these are examples of plants you can and should tackle this time of year, there are also plants that should not be trimmed now.

As a good general rule, you can trim back damaged, dead, or diseased stems and branches from any plant at any time of year. However, harder maintenance pruning needs careful timing. These plants are examples of those that can take a hard trim as winter is about to set in. Most importantly, know which plants and varieties you have and what the best practices are for these before you begin any pruning project.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your dog, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your canine companion.

âHaveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

I purchased my Havanese, Paisley, at 8 weeks. She hasnât eaten any food for three weeks now. That makes her blood sugar drop. I have taken her to the emergency vets twice and my regular vet numerous times.

They have run multiple liver tests but can't find anything wrong with her. I have been hand-feeding her the prescription sugar water the vet gave me, but I have to force her mouth open to give it to her.

Have you ever heard of anything like this?â

A tiny puppy has limited energy reserves, so when she stops eating, her blood glucose can fall quickly. This is one reason we normally feed puppies several times throughout the day. However, three weeks without eating is much more concerning than simple âpuppy hypoglycemia.â Sadly, once a puppy stops eating, this can become a vicious cycle because low blood glucose can cause weakness, abnormal behavior, and even less interest in food. Sugar can temporarily raise her blood glucose, but it does not address the underlying problem. And since Paisley has been refusing food for several weeks, this deserves some serious detective work.

Normal liver blood tests are reassuring, but they do not completely rule out every condition that can cause chronic inappetence or recurrent hypoglycemia in a puppy. Depending on what has already been evaluated, your veterinarian may also consider additional investigation for conditions such as infection, gastrointestinal disease, congenital portosystemic shunting, adrenal disease, or other metabolic disorders.

A portosystemic shunt (PSS) is an abnormal blood vessel that allows some blood from the digestive system to bypass the liver instead of passing through it normally. Because the liver plays an important role in processing nutrients and maintaining normal metabolism, this abnormal circulation can cause problems in some puppies. More specialized blood tests and imaging, such as abdominal ultrasound with Doppler evaluation or, in some cases, CT angiography, may be needed to investigate these conditions.

The Havanese is among the breeds with a higher risk of PSS, so if it hasnât already, I think this should be thoroughly investigated.

Although managing her glucose levels is very important, please be cautious;  forcing sugar water into her mouth carries a risk of aspiration (inhaling the liquid into the lungs). If Paisley is conscious and able to swallow normally, the recommendation is to place a small amount of an appropriate glucose source, like the water you mentioned, directly onto her gums or inside her cheek, where it can be absorbed through the mucous membranes. This can help raise her glucose levels without the risk of aspiration. However, if she becomes extremely weak, cannot swallow normally, collapses, becomes unconscious, or has a seizure, nothing should be given by mouth because of the risk of inhaling it into the lungs. Those situations require immediate emergency veterinary treatment.

Because Paisley has gone this long without eating voluntarily and continues to experience low blood glucose, I would discuss referral to a veterinary internal medicine specialist or hospitalization for nutritional and glucose support. Think of the glucose as a power generator keeping the lights on, but the priority is still finding out why the electrical system keeps failing. Sugar can keep the lights on for a while, but eventually we need to find the faulty wiring. Supporting her blood glucose is essential, but identifying and treating the underlying cause is what will ultimately allow her to maintain normal glucose without constant intervention.

I wish you and Paisley the very best, and I hope this helps.

#7901. 6 ways to make mornings smoother when your child has ADHD

Home / Health & Wellness / Children's Health

A child psychiatrist on the small systems that take the pressure off the hardest 20 minutes of the day.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 15, 2026

It’s 7:40, the bus comes at 7:52, and one shoe is missing. You’ve asked about the backpack four times. Your kid is half-dressed on the floor, watching dust move through a sunbeam.

If that’s your morning, you have company. About 1 in 9 US children, roughly 7.1 million kids, has been diagnosed with ADHD, according to CDC data. For a lot of those families, the hardest stretch of the day happens before anyone heads out the door.

There’s a reason mornings hit this hard, and it isn’t that your kid doesn’t care. Michael Morse, MD, a board-certified child and adolescent psychiatrist who directs the ADHD & Anxiety Center at Alvord Baker and is an associate professor of psychiatry at Georgetown University, says the morning routine requires a child “to do the most with the least help.” Many kids with ADHD run on a later internal clock, he says, so at 7 a.m. the brain regions that handle planning and time aren’t fully up and running, and yet, that’s when we ask kids to move through a string of boring steps against a deadline.

Executive function, the mental system for getting started, tracking time and shifting gears, tends to develop more slowly in kids with ADHD, so what looks like refusal is often a brain that can’t get itself going yet without help. “Kids do well when they can,” Morse says. For parents, that means making a mental shift from asking why your kid won’t do something to examining what’s getting in the way. That reframe can often help you resist a lecture and lend a hand instead. “Punishment can’t teach a skill a child doesn’t have yet,” he says, “but support can.”

“The best mornings usually start the evening before, when there’s time to think and nobody is racing the bus,” Morse says. Sign the permission slips, settle on what’s for breakfast, and, if your kid is old enough, have them pack their backpack and lay out clothes for the next day. (For younger kids, you’ll want to supervise this process.)

He also suggests a five-minute planning talk earlier in the day to look at what’s ahead for the day together, whether that’s gym, a test or a game after school, which helps a kid build their own sense of what’s coming.

Sleep is the biggest lever of all. “A tired brain makes every ADHD symptom worse,” Morse says, and it gets less benefit from medication. Sleep trouble is common here, affecting as many as half of kids with ADHD by some estimates. A steady bedtime, screens off about an hour before bed, and a warm bath or shower all make it easier for your child to nod off at night, which sets the stage for smoother mornings.

Kids with ADHD often can’t hold a string of instructions in mind, so “‘go get ready’ is really six instructions in three words,” Morse says. A visual sequence takes that load off their memory. In practice it’s a simple chart on the bathroom mirror listing each step in order: get dressed, eat breakfast, brush teeth, shoes on, backpack. Use pictures for younger kids and let them check off each step as they go, and build the chart together, since kids are more likely to follow a plan they helped make.

When your kid stalls, skip the fresh reminder and point back to the list with a quick “What’s next on your chart?” Do it long enough and “the chart becomes the reminder instead of the parent,” Morse says.

Many kids with ADHD experience time differently, something “called ‘time blindness,’ though some people prefer not to use that term,” Morse says. Either way, 10 minutes from now and an hour from now can feel about the same, so the tools that help are the ones that make time visible. A visual timer with a colored disk that shrinks as the minutes run out lets a kid see at a glance how much is left, and timers that announce the minutes work well for a kid dressing in another room.

Morse says “a simple timer that does one thing beats a phone,” since phones are designed to pull attention toward games and messages, the opposite of what a kid needs while getting ready.

Every choice in the morning is another chance to stall, and each stall may need an adult to jump-start things again. So take the decisions out ahead of time. Have your child select their outfit the night before or keep a few go-to options on rotation. “Some kids wear something close to a uniform and are relieved not to have to think about it,” Morse says. For breakfast, offer two pre-approved options, ideally with some protein like eggs or yogurt to keep energy steady throughout the day.

Give the backpack, shoes and jacket a single launch spot, one basket or hook where they always live, so nobody’s hunting a missing shoe at 7:40. The thread running through all of it, in Morse’s words, is “moving the thinking out of the morning and into the calm of the evening. Fewer decisions also mean fewer arguments.”

If your kid takes medication, when they take it can matter as much as whether they take it. “No ADHD medicine works the moment it’s swallowed,” Morse says, so a long-acting stimulant taken at breakfast may not kick in until a child is already at school, leaving the hardest part of the morning uncovered. Some families, with their doctor’s guidance, give the dose closer to wake-up so it has more time to start working, and some formulations are made to be taken the night before.

This one is a conversation for your prescriber rather than a change to make on your own. Timing is one factor that can impact a medication’s efficacy, so it’s worth raising at the next appointment.

“A few fixes come from love and still backfire,” Morse says. Dressing a dawdling second grader or racing a forgotten worksheet to school smooths the morning but teaches a kid they can’t manage on their own. Repeatedly raising your voice tends to pull everyone into a louder and louder standoff. And consequences rarely do the teaching, because “the problem was memory, not caring,” Morse says.

When a morning does come apart, the goal is to keep it from becoming a bad day between you and your kid. Once everyone’s out the door, the moment for teaching has passed, and a lecture in the car just sends a child into school ashamed and anxious. Try something simple instead, like “That was a rough morning. I love you, and we’ll figure it out.”

Later, when everyone’s calm, look at what broke together, since it’s usually one step you can fix without overhauling the whole routine. Go easy on yourself too. (And if you need a bit of support, Morse points parents to the work of psychologist Kristin Neff on self-compassion.)

None of this makes mornings frictionless. It hands the remembering to a system instead of to you, so you’re not the last thing standing between your kid and the 7:52 bus.

Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A plant frost jacket is such a simple, straightforward way to keep plants alive and well over winter, and modern designs with drawstring bases and ventilating zips make it easier than ever to use them. When winterizing a garden, zippered plant jackets don’t only protect tender beauties like banana plants and tree ferns but can help to stop sensitive souls like olive trees from dropping their leaves in a cold snap, shield citrus trees from the occasional frost if you garden in zone 9, and prevent palms from rotting.

Fleece plant covers are also incredibly useful to cocoon early-blooming shrubs like camellia and magnolia if a frost hits just as they’re setting their buds, so you can save the flower show. Young fruit trees, too, can benefit from this extra layer to stop their thin bark splitting in freezing winter conditions, and a plant cover can shield all sorts of other plants from damage caused by snow, sleet and strong winds.

So, if you're getting ready to winterize plants as you prepare your garden for the onset of cold weather, plant jackets should be part of your plan. Not all fleece plant covers are created equal, however, so if you want them to actually work, you need to take a close look at their weight rating. The material used to make frost jackets comes in different weights and, just like comforters offer various levels of warmth, that directly impacts how well it will protect plants in winter, but also the more sunshine it'll block.

Horticultural fleece is a non-woven material typically made from polypropylene, and its weight determines how much protection it offers your plant, measured in grams per square meter (gsm) or ounces per square yard (oz/sq yd). Check the label or online description to find the rating. Any good-quality frost jacket will state the rating and the higher the number, the more insulation it will provide but also block more sunlight.

Armed with this knowledge, you can choose the exact right level of protection for whatever plant you’re winterizing in your USDA zone. While you need to ensure your plant is getting the right level of cold protection, you also need to cater for its sunlight needs.

Because these plants are dormant through winter in colder zones, they don’t need sunlight so you can safely use an ultra heavy-weight fleece to protect them. The fleece alone won’t be enough to protect banana plants (Musa basjoo) and tree ferns (Dicksonia antarctica) from the deep chill of colder zones but are still useful as a cover once you’ve packed layers of insulating straw around the plant. Not only will the fleece form a great barrier against wind and rain but it’ll keep the straw in place and that wrapped plant looking tidy.

Made from 95gsm or 2.8oz/sq yd non-woven material, these plant covers have rounded tops for a good fit and come in green, beige or white in four sizes: 31" x 25", 47" x 39", 71" x 47" and 94" x 79".

Because deciduous shrubs drop their leaves in fall, they don’t need any sunlight over winter to survive so you can safely zip them up in a heavy or ultra heavy-weight plant jacket, depending on the level of protection needed in your zone. This thicker material will also keep snow from weighing down and snapping brittle winter branches. Do choose a design with a zipper as well as a base drawstring so you can regularly open up the zip on milder days to let air circulate.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In 60gsm or 1.77oz/sq yd non-woven fabric, these zippered plant jackets are made of a minimum 50% recycled material and come in four sizes: 23" x 23", 39" x 31", 71" x 47" and 83" x 71".

Hardy shrubs that flower early in the spring such as camellias and magnolias are typically tough enough to survive most winters without a jacket, but their flowerbuds are quickly killed by a late frost or cold snap. Throw on a medium- or heavy-weight plant jacket overnight to save those new buds from the frost.

Evergreen plants such as conifers still need sunlight and fresh air to survive through winter, so a medium-weight fleece is your best bet for general winterizing if your aim is to shield a hardy plant from snow, hail and wind damage. If you’re planning on leaving it on permanently through winter, use a medium-duty fleece for more tender evergreen olive and citrus trees and certain palms, too.

However, if you live in a colder climate you’ll need the increased protection of a heavy- or ultra heavy-weight fleece for these more tender plants. Either use this as an extra layer to throw on over the top of the permanent medium-weight layer in severe weather or, if you use this as the mainstay cover, you’ll need to keep unzipping it to allow sunshine and air in during milder daytime temperatures.

Most medium-duty fleeces are designed without a zipper but that’s not a problem: because the thinner material lets more air and sunlight through, they can safely be left in place.

Made of 32gsm or 0.95oz/sq yd breathable material, this medium-weight plant cover has a drawstring base and is available in three sizes: 32" x 32", 55" x 48" and 72" x 72".

No fleece jacket can generate heat, it can only insulate from the cold, so how you use it has a huge impact on how effectively it protects your plant in winter. Choose a design with both a drawstring and a zip as this not only makes the jacket quick and easy to pop on, but allows you to fit it closely and avoids the wind ripping it off.

Wherever possible, peg the plant jacket to the ground to catch any heat rising upwards. Soil holds onto considerable warmth from the sun, so make use of this natural radiator. Use bricks or stones to weigh the jacket base down, or peg it to the ground with landscape fabric pegs, choosing a product with gaskets to prevent the fabric tearing like these Galvanized Landscape Pins from Amazon.

Similarly, if you’re winterizing a plant in a container, use a frost jacket that’s big enough to fit around the pot, too, as this will protect the roots as well as trap any heat from the soil. Roots in planters are very vulnerable to freezing temperatures so consider wrapping the pot with bubble wrap first.

To prevent moisture building up under the cover and causing mold, make sure you buy a jacket marked as breathable, and open the zip on mild days to allow air to circulate.

While you don’t want to squash a plant into a cover, it’s a wise idea to fit the jacket around the plant to prevent it flapping in the wind and metal greenhouse clamps such as these from Amazon are invaluable to gather loose material or clip a jacket to existing plant supports.

Measuring 8’ x 8’ to fit bigger shrubs and trees, this ultra heavy-weight 80gsm or 2.4oz/yd cover comes with ties and stakes so it can be pinned securely to the ground in exposed gardens.

These ultra heavy-weight zippered covers are made from 75gsm or 2.2oz/sq yd patterned fabric and are available in a green or grey print in sizes 32"x24", 47"x32", 71"x47" and 83"x71".

Shaped for wide, bushy shrubs, this heavy-weight plant cover made of 50gsm or 1.5oz/sq yd fabric measures a generous 7' x 7' and is also available in an 8' square size.

Since 2001, October 16th has been known as National Feral Cat Day â an opportunity to raise awareness about community cats (also called feral or stray), promote Trap-Neuter-Return, and give a voice to the millions of caring people who dedicate their time and energy to improving the lives of the cats & kittens most in need of support. It is estimated that there are around 60-100 million stray cats in the US, and we know that it takes more than just one day to make a meaningful difference in a problem this overwhelming. Thatâs why many feline rescue groups want to turn Feral Cat Day into Feral Cat Awareness Month.

Leading the charge is Mission Meow, a unique organization that supports small feline-focused nonprofits with impactful grants, helping to deliver lasting transformations for cats in need. Throughout the year, they coordinate with donors to provide much-needed funding to animal charities across the country, giving smaller groups the means to continue their vital work. To celebrate Mission Meowâs 4th Anniversary and #FeralCatAwarenessMonth, the latest round of grant recipients have been selected in recognition of the work they do to address one of the biggest challenges facing cat rescue: overpopulation.

One of the most impactful initiatives in managing stray and feral cat communities is Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR).

âTNR tackles the problem at its source by humanely reducing the number of kittens being born outdoors while improving the lives of existing community cats,â says Sally Williams, founder and CEO of Mission Meow. âWith our anniversary falling during Feral Cat Awareness Month, it felt like the perfect opportunity to shine a light on this critical work and invest in organizations creating long-term, sustainable change.â

With that in mind, five nonprofit organizations were selected for this round of Mission Meow grants:

Community Cat Welfare Network in Pinehurst, North Carolina supports the humane welfare and stabilization of existing community cat colonies in central North Carolina through the provision of food, insulated winter shelters, veterinary care, humane population stabilization efforts, and public education.

Grant funding will provide 20 winter shelters for stabilized community cat colonies.

Through the work of Fix & Feed Feline Feral in Tampa, Florida, stray cats and kittens are humanely trapped and spayed or neutered, vaccinated for rabies, and returned to their colonies, which are managed by caring volunteers. The health of these feline communities is supported through health checkups, annual vaccinations, and specific health care as needed.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment and an incubator to expand their growing community program.

Lupa Legacy Animal Rescue provides medical care to homeless pets in central Oklahoma, with a focus on owner-surrendered pets and tame, stray cats and kittens from TNR efforts.

Grant funding will help provide TNR equipment and microchip readers to expand trapping efforts to a nearby trailer park.

Hands to Paws Rescue in Georgia initiates and supports programs that extend and elevate the standards of compassionate care for companion animals in the greater Augusta area by providing educational programs, direct care, and cooperative efforts to increase access to low-cost spay/neuter, rescue, fostering, and adoption of animals.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to help expand their community cat spay/neuter transportation program.

TippedEars in Compton, California, is combating cat overpopulation through humane TNR. While in their care, community cats are sterilized, vaccinated, and treated for fleas.

Grant funding supports TNR equipment to create a trap-lending program for trained community members.

Each organization stood out in its own unique way, but they all shared qualities that are deeply important to Mission Meow. They are collaborative, community-focused, and committed to TNR, addressing cat overpopulation at its source. Many work with underserved communities and focus on community cats who could easily be overlooked. Most importantly, they understand that creating lasting change means not only helping the cats in front of us today, but also working to prevent more cats from needing help tomorrow.

Even little changes can have a huge impact, and there is no such thing as a âsmallâ donation â every little bit helps. Start at home by supporting local animal shelters and TNR programs, spay & neuter your cats, and when youâre looking for a new feline friend, think adoption first.

#7897. Dogs on the Screen and in the Audience for Brad Pitt’s New Film

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

You know the drill. Keys in hand. Shoes on. One last look at your dog before you head out, and there they are, wagging their tail like maybe, just maybe, this time you are taking them with you.

Those hopeful eyes. That little head tilt. The expression that says, Excuse me, where exactly do you think youâre going without me?

And then you do the cruelest thing imaginable: you leave.

Sure, they have a perfectly comfortable sofa at home, but imagine settling into a movie theater seat, popcorn in hand, with your dog curled up beside you. Instead of leaving them behind, wondering where you went, you could reach down during the movie and give them a little scratch behind the ears.

Honestly, why have we been doing movie night without them all this time?

Apparently, someone in Miami had the same thought.

At a special screening of Brad Pittâs new movie, Heart of the Beast, at Silverspot Cinema in Downtown Miami on September 19, dogs were officially on the invite list.

The morning had all the ingredients of a proper dog outing: leashes in the lobby, photo ops, plenty of new butts to sniff, and a red carpet where the dogs seemed perfectly comfortable stealing the spotlight.

Then came the part that made this movie night different. The dogs got to go inside and watch the movie, too. And considering that Heart of the Beast is about the bond between a man and his dog, enjoying it in the company of dogs feels almost too perfect.

Heart of the Beast follows Special Forces officer James Belmont, played by Brad Pitt, and his combat dog, Odin, after a plane crash leaves them stranded in the Alaskan wilderness. Their survival depends on communication, trust, and their ability to work together.

The story centers on a relationship that many dog people will recognize, even if the circumstances are a bit more dramatic than the average Tuesday with a Labrador!

Directed by David Ayer and co-starring a German Shepherd named Uber, the movie is described as an adventure thriller centered on the bond between a man and his dog as they face the Alaskan wilderness together.

So while the movie tells the story of one extraordinary human-dog partnership, the Miami screening gave plenty of ordinary dog parents the chance to celebrate their own.

And really, that is part of what makes dogs such irresistible companions. They are not just waiting at home while life happens. They are woven into the little things: the walks, the errands, the road trips, the lazy Sunday mornings; even the occasional movie date.

As fun as dogs in the theater sounds, not every dog is going to be thrilled about it. Crowds, darkness, unfamiliar dogs, and those big cinematic sound effects can be a lot, especially for pups who are sensitive to noise.

Dogs hear much more acutely than we do, so a theater that feels exciting to us can feel pretty intense to them. Around 90 decibels can be uncomfortable for some dogs, and sudden bursts of sound can be especially startling.

A pup who settles happily beside their person? Perfect.

A pup who starts panting, pacing, hiding, or searching for the exit? That is probably their polite way of saying, âI vote for the sofa.â

And honestly, that is okay. Dog-friendly should mean dog-comfortable, not dog-compulsory.

The movie promotion had another very good reason to put dogs in the spotlight.

Ahead of the filmâs September 25 theatrical release, Brad Pitt teamed up with organizations including Wags & Walks Nashville to bring adoptable rescue dogs along to some of the movieâs promotional events.

At a Big Dog Adoption Event in Nashville, Pitt and animal coordinator Andrew Simpson spent time with dogs looking for homes. And at the filmâs global premiere in Franklin, Tennessee, adoptable dogs from Wags & Walks got to join Pitt on the red carpet.

And letâs face it, standing beside Brad Pitt is only going to improve a dogâs chances of finding a new home! Itâs the kind of exposure that can give a little rescue dog a better chance of being noticed. Someone who has never considered adopting might spot one of those faces, click to find out more, and suddenly find themselves filling out the adoption paperwork.

And that is perhaps the most impactful part of all this movie promotion.

The movie gives us a story about the bond between a man and his dog. For these rescue dogs, the hope is much simpler: to find their person, go home, and become someoneâs dog. If Brad Pittâs star power helps a few of these dogs find their forever home, that has to be worth more than any gold statuette.

For the dogs who got to tag along in Miami, they got the kind of movie night most dogs can only dream about: their person right beside them, plenty of new smells to investigate, and a whole theater full of things to sniff. Add a little popcorn to the mix, and honestly, what more could a dog ask for?

#7896. 6 Tips For Getting Through The Holidays When You’re A Mom With ADHD

Strategies for ditching the burnout, surviving the chaos, and rediscovering holiday magic.

Kids losing sleep during the holidays basically a rite of passage. But for moms with ADHD? By that point, the holiday sleep deprivation started weeks ago.

Here’s how mom-of-two Alba C. puts it: “[During the holidays] my mind races to the point that it can take me hours to fall asleep, or fall back asleep. I’ll have thoughts like, ‘Did I buy enough presents?,’ and ‘I have so many presents to wrap!’ Those thoughts start piling up, and that can put me in a moody state where I get irritated very easily.”

Nobody wants to be the holiday Grinch. But when you toss executive dysfunction into the mix with social obligations, family drama, and midnight present-wrapping marathons, the holidays become a brutal obstacle course for moms with ADHD.

“Mothers are often responsible for much of the invisible labor associated with the holidays, from coordinating family schedules, to purchasing and wrapping gifts, moving the Elf on a Shelf, making the ‘holiday magic,’ and keeping a pulse on everyone’s logistical and emotional needs,” explains neuropsychologist Dr. Jessica McCarthy. “For women with ADHD, these responsibilities can become especially overwhelming.”

So moms with ADHD, hear this: You aren’t failing at the holidays — they’re just intense. We talked to experts — and some moms who’ve been through it — to find out how to ditch the burnout, survive the chaos, and rediscover holiday magic this season. Here are some ways to cope.

The holidays amplify struggles with executive dysfunction like forgetfulness, task avoidance, or missing details, explains Dr. Ifeanyi M. Olele, a board-certified psychiatrist with Genesis Psychiatric Solutions. To ease holiday stress, he recommends delegating responsibilities to other family members and asking for help wherever possible.

“Moms shouldn't feel that they have to do everything themselves. If you have a spouse or partner, communicate and divide responsibilities. If there are teenagers or adult children in the house, ask them to help with some of the holiday preparations,” he says.

Holiday parties are where Jacquelyn D.’s ADHD symptoms — including sound sensitivity and social self-consciousness — feel the most intense. To avoid spoiling the party, the 47-year-old mom of two always comes prepared with an escape plan.

“I take a break when I need to, and don't feel bad taking a few minutes to regulate myself,” she explains. “I have some social masking techniques as well, like keeping conversations short and directed outward, and using checking on the kids as a reason to step away and get some fresh air.”

During the merriest season, many moms stay up late wrapping gifts, organizing events, or completing tasks they couldn’t get to during the day. Since sleep deprivation magnifies difficulties women with ADHD are already working hard to manage — like attention, working memory, impulse control, and emotional regulation — Dr. McCarthy advises that sometimes the most productive thing a mom can do is leave something unfinished, and go to bed.

“My advice is to treat sleep as a priority rather than something that happens after everything else is finished,” says McCarthy. “Set realistic cutoff times for holiday tasks, maintain consistent sleep routines when possible, and resist the pressure to sacrifice rest to meet unrealistic expectations.”

One of the biggest mistakes busy moms make during the holiday season is assuming that because there’s technically room on the calendar for another activity, they have the emotional capacity for it, explains Kristen Carder, an ADHD coach and author of You're Not in Trouble: The ADHD Guide to Building Healthy, Connected Relationships.

“If you know that an afternoon with extended family is going to be emotionally taxing, don't schedule another demanding activity immediately afterward. Build in downtime, protect your routines when possible, and pay attention to early signs of dysregulation.”

Amy H., an author and mother of eight, keeps her own ADHD symptoms in check by planning ahead. Her advice? Start your preparations early. Like, early, early.

“Start earlier than feels reasonable,” Amy recommends. “ If the prep is done early, December gets to be about the good stuff instead of the panic. Your future self will thank you — and so will everyone who has to live with that future self.”

While social media scrolls portrays picture-perfect holiday decor and flawless family photos, Emily M., a mom of five, reminds us that real life is rarely as immaculate as it appears through tiny screens — especially for moms with ADHD.

“When I feel myself starting to spiral and feel like I’m not enough, I look at my husband, my kids, and my friends, and I remind myself that I’m worthy even when I’m not perfect. Some days I have to come back to that over and over again, and that’s okay,” she says. “That is the practice.”

Learn more about how to handle your ADHD symptoms at https://www.reframeadhd.com/

#7895. Flu season is early this year. Here’s how to actually protect your family, according to experts

For real advice, we talked to two physicians who've spent this fall fielding questions from worried parents.

By Sara Goldstein Updated Oct. 16, 2026

It’s almost that time of year when a small cornucopia of medicine takes up residence on the kitchen counter and the house becomes a chorus of coughs and sneezes. As a parent, you know the particular dread of seeing the school nurse’s number flashing on your phone, because you know it’s only a matter of hours until the whole family is flat out.

Unfortunately that call may be right around the corner: Flu season is also arriving months earlier than usual this year.

Experts say it’s a good idea to prepare now before the first fever strikes. Most of what actually protects a family is simple, though, and you don’t need a cabinet full of products or a nursing degree to do it well.

For real advice, we talked to two physicians who’ve spent this fall fielding questions from worried parents. Tracy Tyson, MD and Brittany Odom, MD, are both board-certified pediatricians and moms themselves. Here’s what they want you to know about how to protect your family from the flu this season.

Yes, in parts of the country. “We have started seeing influenza earlier this year, and nationwide reports are also showing an earlier flu season,” Dr. Tyson says. The picture is uneven, though. “Nationally, the latest CDC report shows flu activity is still relatively low but increasing, with the highest activity on the West Coast,” Dr. Odom says, and she’s already seeing plenty of cases in her area. Regions surge at slightly different times, she says, reason enough to get ahead of it now. “You don’t need to wait for flu to fill your child’s classroom before getting them protected.”

Get it as soon as it’s available, both doctors say. “I recommend getting it in September or October, ideally by Halloween, for everyone 6 months and older,” Dr. Odom says. November isn’t too late, she adds, but she wouldn’t wait on purpose, since protection takes about 2 weeks to build and some kids ages 6 months through 8 years need 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart.

“It isn’t ever too late, but the earlier, the better,” Dr. Tyson says. The flu and COVID shots can be given at the same visit, with no required spacing. “As a mom, I know how quickly something on the calendar can get pushed back,” Dr. Odom adds. “So if you have the opportunity now, take it.”

Either one works, if your child is eligible, both doctors say. The shot is approved for children 6 months and up. The nasal spray, or flu mist, is an option from age 2, with limits. “Children ages 2 through 4 with asthma or wheezing in the past year shouldn’t receive the nasal spray, and older children with asthma or other medical conditions need an eligibility review,” Dr. Odom says. Dr. Tyson draws the same line for the mist. Past that, it comes down to your kid. “My priority is an appropriate vaccine that your child actually receives,” Dr. Odom says.

The shot lowers the odds of catching the flu and softens its severity when it breaks through. Dr. Tyson likes an old health-department line. “Taking flu from wild to mild is exactly the right way of thinking,” she says, estimating it prevents flu in up to 60% of cases. It targets influenza specifically, not the parade of other bugs your kid hauls home from daycare. “A sick day after vaccination doesn’t mean the vaccine had no value,” Dr. Odom says, since even a vaccinated child who gets the flu is less likely to end up seriously ill.

If one kid goes down, the rest of the house doesn’t necessarily have to fall like dominos. You absolutely can limit the spread, Dr. Tyson says. The moves that help are unglamorous. Wash hands, stop sharing cups and utensils, cough into an elbow, and separate sleeping spaces where you can. Vaccination cuts household spread too.

You don’t need to disinfect every surface. “Don’t put all your energy into wiping down the house while overlooking the air everyone is sharing,” Dr. Odom says. Crack a window, run a HEPA air purifier, or run the HVAC fan while someone is sick. Masks help during close contact, though never on a child under 2.

And it’s not a failure if another family member gets sick.. “Viruses are sneaky, it happens,” Dr. Odom says.

Most healthy, older kids can ride out the flu at home, but call your doctor if:

Keep a few basics on hand, Dr. Odom says: a thermometer, an oral rehydration solution like Pedialyte, saline drops or spray, and an age-appropriate fever medicine with a dosing syringe. An at-home combination test (which generally covers flu A and B, COVID and RSV in one swab) can also help you tell the flu from the other bugs going around. Care itself is mostly rest, small frequent sips of fluid and saline for congestion. For babies, keep offering breast milk or formula. Honey can soothe a cough for kids 1 and older, but never for a baby under 1.

For fever and aches, acetaminophen helps, and ibuprofen is fine from 6 months, though skip it if your child is dehydrated or vomiting a lot, Dr. Odom says. Dose by weight and use the syringe, not a kitchen spoon, she adds, and never give aspirin to a child with flu.

On how high is too high, the number matters less than you’d think. “There isn’t a level of fever that is unsafe per se,” Dr. Tyson says. “It’s more about the length of time and the symptoms with the fever.” Call the doctor for a baby under 3 months at 100.4°F or higher, and for an older child whose fever repeatedly tops 104°F or won’t come down with medicine. The goal, Dr. Odom says, is a child comfortable enough to drink and rest.

The most vulnerable people in a house can’t protect themselves, so the job falls on everyone else. Babies under 6 months are too young for the flu vaccine, which makes vaccinating the adults and older kids at home especially important, Dr. Odom says. Keep sick visitors away, improve airflow, and for newborns, the advice is obvious but still worth stating since the desire is strong: “No kissing the babies!” The flu shot is safe in any trimester of pregnancy and protects the baby after birth too. For anyone pregnant, immunocompromised or caring for a newborn, don’t wait out a symptom or a known exposure. Call your provider promptly about treatment or prevention.

Asked what they most wish parents knew, both doctors have the same advice: reach out sooner. “You don’t have to wait until your child looks terribly sick to call us,” Dr. Odom says. “Flu has treatments, and timing matters. Asking for help early is part of taking good care of your child, not overreacting.”

They’re so good, you’re gonna need some extra willpower not to open all the doors at once.

Let’s give credit where credit is due: Advent calendars have gotten really good. The flimsy cardboard boxes of subpar waxy chocolate squares from our childhood have been usurped by countdowns that truly feel like a special way to treat yourself all the way up to Dec. 25.

There are calendars that build a full art kit. Those that give you a tailor-made excuse to top off your wine glass every afternoon. Whether you’re shopping for a toy-obsessed kid, a stationery girlie, or yourself (ain’t no shame in our game), there’s a countdown here that’ll make the days leading up to Christmas kinda feel like the main event instead of the warm-up.

An important PSA before you scroll, though: the good ones tend to sell out fast, often well before Dec. 1. So if something catches your eye, add it to your cart ASAP and thank us later.

An advent calendar that comes with a new mini storybook every single day is the kind of holiday magic that makes December feel genuinely special from the very first of the month. Each of the 24 doors reveals a different illustrated Christmas story, which means the countdown to Christmas doubles as a reading ritual and an excuse to snuggle up together every night before bed. It’s the most meaningful advent calendar upgrade for any family that loves books and wants the holidays to feel a little more intentional and a lot more cozy. — Katie Garrity, Senior Editor, News & Social

For the chocolate lover in your life, consider getting them the See's Candies advent calendar. It comes stocked with over a pound of chocolate (yum), in a variety of totally delicious flavors. Even better, this calendar is 3-D, and is created to look like a vintage candy shop. How adorable AND delicious! — Kate Auletta, Editor in Chief

This is one of those advent calendars where you just send your partner the link without any other information and hope for the best. While your kids can enjoy their silly little chocolates, you can get down with this super-luxury jewelry countdown. The calendar includes very classic but fun earrings, necklaces, charms, and bracelets in either gold or silver, and there's not a single piece I wouldn't wear. — Sarah Aswell, Deputy Editor, News & Social

Almost every advent calendar that comes through our door ends up being absconded with by my kids, which is maybe why I’m so excited about this one: It’s just for me! Behind its 12 doors are FULL-SIZE deluxe goodies that go above and beyond a typical beauty calendar. We’re talking a Blissy silk sleep mask, a cozy UnHide amber candle... even a pair of Leeada stud earrings. It’s like a curated holiday shopping spree just for moms. — Julie Sprankles, Deputy Editor, Lifestyle & Entertainment

This is the advent calendar for the family who wants something genuinely hilarious and slightly unhinged. The Brass Monkey Googly-Eyed Magnet Countdown is a 25-day magnetic calendar where each day reveals a new googly-eyed character or scene that sticks to the board and builds into a progressively more chaotic and delightful holiday display. It is reusable year after year, requires zero chocolate or candy, and is the kind of calendar that gets the whole family involved in peeling back each day just to see what ridiculous thing comes next. — Katie Garrity

This advent calendar is not only so pretty to look at, it also comes stocked with all kinds of fragrances, eau de parfum, and bath and body products (including the brand’s Perfume Pencils, which only come out at the holidays). There's also a Christmas ornament and a coffee table book included. I love a good fragrance — on my hands or wafting through my kitchen; this calendar is a welcome addition to my home. — Kate Auletta

I’m treating myself to this advent calendar because I am a stationery girlie, and an advent calendar filled with 24 doors of Papier goodies is genuinely the most excited I get about December. Each door reveals a different surprise — think notecards, stickers, mini notebooks, and other beautifully designed paper goods — which means the countdown to Christmas also doubles as slowly building up a stash of the most charming little stationery pieces. It’s the advent calendar for the person who has everything but will always find room for one more beautiful notecard set! — Katie Garrity

My 15-year-old and I had a blast going halfsies with this beauty lover’s advent calendar. The clear makeup case (love that the “calendar” can be reused) holds individually packaged surprises like SHEGLAM’s lip stains and blushes and highlighters and glosses. Every product is good enough to go straight into the daily beauty rotation! — Julie Sprankles

For the kid who is obsessed with Magna-Tiles, this advent calendar is going to completely send them into orbit. Each of the 24 doors reveals a new micro magnetic tile piece that adds to their collection, and by Christmas morning they have a full 34-piece microMAGS set ready to build with. It is an advent calendar that is also a gift, which is the smartest possible use of December and makes the whole month feel like one long unwrapping experience. — Katie Garrity

Who doesn't want a boatload of beauty products every day for a month? This is a high-end calendar, sure, but it's worth it. It comes with a lovely grouping of all kinds of products, and makes a great gift for the beauty-obsessed person (it's me, hi) in your life. — Kate Auletta

I have so many memories from my own childhood of reading Little Golden Books, so this advent calendar feels especially sentimental. Behind each of the 24 windows is a mini paperback Little Golden Book, gold-foil spines and all, with a full story and original art. Opening a new book every night and reading it with your little ones sounds like such a sweet bedtime ritual for December, doesn’t it? — Julie Sprankles

Each of the 24 windows of this absolutely gorgeous advent calendar hides a gourmet chocolate, and those little chocolates are truly delicious. This year’s lineup even includes a limited-edition milk chocolate bonbon with candied orange and holiday spices, aka Christmas in a bite. The whole thing is practically pretty enough to double as decor, too. — Julie Sprankles

Now, this is the advent calendar for ME, and I will not be taking questions about it. Each door reveals a different 187ml pour — reds, whites, rosés, and bubbles — from a curated selection of wines that are actually good rather than the bottom-shelf stuff you tolerate, which means December doubles as a month-long wine discovery experience. — Katie Garrity

When I saw that IPSY’s advent calendar consisted of 25 days of beauty surprises from brands I know and love like Glow Recipe, Gisou, and more, I knew it needed to be part of our holidays this year. If you’re gifting, it’s such an easy grab for the beauty lover on your list! I also appreciate that you don’t need an IPSY membership to order one, making it a great little trial run if you’ve been on the fence about joining. — Julie Sprankles

An advent calendar that doubles as a fully stocked art supply haul? YES! Each of the 24 doors reveals a different Ohuhu art supply, including markers, colored pencils, brush pens, and more, so by Christmas she has an entire professional-quality art kit built one piece at a time. Ohuhu is a brand that serious artists actually love and recommend, which means these are not cheap throwaway supplies but tools she will actually use long after December is over. — Katie Garrity

The classic chocolate advent calendar gets a serious upgrade with Lindt. Instead of the thin, waxy chocolate squares that come with most calendars, each door reveals a Lindt Teddy Bear or other premium Lindt chocolate, which is the kind of daily December treat that actually makes the countdown feel special. It is the advent calendar that works for every age, requires zero assembly, and makes everyone in the house immediately invested in what is behind each door. Sometimes the simplest idea done really well is the best idea, and this is exactly that! — Katie Garrity

I’m clearly a sucker for a pre-filled advent calendar, but I always make room on a tabletop or my mantel for one we stock ourselves. This year, that spot belongs to this charming little house from At Home that looks like it came straight out of a Christmas village. We’re going to surround this with some greenery and twinkle lights, and I’m thinking I might fill it with a mix of candy pieces and little notes... or maybe family activities for us to do next year. — Julie Sprankles

#7892. The Silent Health Problem Vets Say Most Cat Owners Never See Coming

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Dental disease is one of the most common health problems seen by vets, yet it's also one of the easiest to overlook. Cats are particularly good at hiding discomfort, so a cat with painful teeth or inflamed gums may carry on behaving normally for a surprisingly long time.

By the time obvious signs appear, the problem may already have been developing for months or even longer, and suddenly a minor issue is a major disaster. The good news is that dental disease is largely preventable, and keeping a cat's teeth healthy doesn't necessarily mean relying on a toothbrush alone.

Plaque is where the problem begins. It forms when bacteria mix with saliva and food particles on the surface of the teeth. If plaque isn't removed, it can harden into tartar â aka calculus â within days.

Tartar leads to inflammation of the gums, a condition known as gingivitis. This can progress to periodontitis, an infection involving the tooth root, weakening the attachment between the gum and the tooth, and eroding enamel. Eventually, the tooth starts breaking down from the inside.

These conditions can all be painful. A cat with advanced dental disease may drool, paw at its mouth, drop food while eating, or stop eating altogether. Bad breath, bloody saliva, teeth chattering, and even sneezing can also be warning signs.

Unfortunately, cats don't always make their discomfort obvious, which is why prevention is so important.

Regular toothbrushing remains the most effective way to prevent dental disease in cats. Daily brushing removes plaque before it has the chance to harden into tartar and tackles one of the main causes of dental problems.

A toothbrush or finger brush designed for cats should be used with toothpaste specifically formulated for felines. Human toothpaste contains ingredients that can be harmful if swallowed.

It's much easier to establish the habit when a cat is young, making it an enjoyable, even fun part of their routine. Older cats can learn too, although a slow approach with plenty of positive reinforcement gives the best chance of success.

Even brushing every few days is better than not brushing at all, although daily brushing provides the greatest benefit.

For cats that arenât tolerating a brush, dental wipes can be a good option.

For cats that won't tolerate brushing, dental diets and treats can provide another option. Dental dry foods contain ingredients and have a texture that are designed to help reduce plaque formation. The limitation is that not every cat actually chews its food. Some cats swallow their food with very little chewing, which reduces the potential benefit.

When choosing dental products, the Veterinary Oral Health Council seal is a useful indicator of effectiveness. Products carrying the VOHC seal have been independently tested and shown to reduce plaque or tartar.

Prescription dental diets are also available through veterinarians. They typically use oversized kibble designed to encourage more contact with the teeth during chewing and may be worth considering for cats with a history of dental problems.

Dental treats and chews have a similar action to dental diets, but are often made from more palatable ingredients to encourage cats to chew them. As a result, they can be quite high in calories, so make sure you include them in your catâs daily allowance.

More recently, powders containing brown algae or seaweed have been showing promising results in the fight against tartar formation, but some cats arenât keen on the taste.

Oral rinses offer another preventative option for cats that resist brushing and aren't suitable for dietary changes. They can be applied using gauze or a soft cloth and work by chemically reducing plaque and tartar before they build up.

The VOHC seal can again help when choosing between products. A veterinarian can also recommend an appropriate rinse for an individual cat.

Water additives are one of the easiest dental care options because they are simply added to a cat's drinking water. They work by helping inhibit plaque formation.

There are some important limitations, however. A cat that doesn't drink enough water may not receive much benefit, while some additives can change the smell or taste of the water enough that a cat avoids drinking it.

A VOHC-approved water additive can be a useful addition to a broader dental care routine, but it is unlikely to be enough on its own.

Plaque prevention gels are often used after a professional dental cleaning. They can help protect newly cleaned teeth and extend the time before another cleaning is needed.

Veterinarians commonly recommend these gels as a follow-up to professional dental treatment rather than as a standalone daily solution. Any instructions about feeding and drinking after application should be followed carefully.

Even cats receiving regular dental care at home may eventually need a professional cleaning. This is performed under general anesthesia, allowing the veterinarian to clean below the gum line, examine each tooth closely, take dental X-rays when necessary, and identify teeth that need to be removed.

The need for anesthesia can understandably concern some owners, but untreated dental disease can lead to chronic pain, infection, and systemic illness.

Senior cats and cats with a history of dental problems may also need their teeth assessed more frequently than during a standard annual examination. Finding problems early generally means treatment can be simpler and less invasive.

There has been a rise in the number of businesses offering dentals without anesthesia, at a price much lower than a dental procedure with your vet. While the idea of a cheaper dental cleaning without the worry of your cat going under anesthetic is appealing, the most significant periodontal disease happens below the gumline. Cats in particular are susceptible to a painful condition known as feline oral resorptive lesions (FORLs), in which the tooth slowly dissolves. FORLs can develop in completely clean teeth. They often form in the roots and need to be diagnosed using dental x-ray.

A catâs teeth may look clean after an anesthetic-free dental, but there could be painful problems going on beneath the surface.

Dental disease isn't inevitable, but preventing it requires more than waiting for obvious symptoms to appear. Cats can hide dental pain remarkably well, meaning a seemingly healthy mouth may already have problems developing beneath the surface.

Regular brushing is the most effective option, but dental diets, treats, rinses, water additives, and professional cleaning can all play a role. The right combination will depend on the individual cat and how well they tolerate each approach.

Keeping on top of dental care can help prevent painful problems from becoming something a cat has to quietly live with for years.

#7891. What’s That Smell??? How To Tell the Difference Between Normal Stinky Dog Breath and A Warning Sign

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

A dog's breath is never going to be minty fresh, but there's a big difference between ordinary doggy breath and an odor that's genuinely foul. A healthy dog's mouth should have a mild smell, often with a faint trace of whatever they last ate. When that smell suddenly becomes fishy, rotten, or unusually unpleasant, it can be a sign that something else is going on.

Bad breath can have several possible causes, ranging from common dental problems to health conditions that need urgent veterinary attention. Knowing what that smell might be telling you can make it easier to recognize when it's time for a closer look.

Periodontal disease is the most common cause of persistent bad breath in dogs. It develops as tartar builds up on the teeth and eventually affects the ligament holding each tooth in place.

The smell can become particularly strong and rotten as the disease progresses. Other signs include inflamed or bleeding gums, loose or missing teeth, heavy tartar, exposed tooth roots, changes in appetite, difficulty chewing, and pawing at the mouth.

Gingivitis is an earlier stage of periodontal disease and causes the gums to become inflamed. Bad breath is often one of the first noticeable signs.

Unlike more advanced periodontal disease, gingivitis is reversible when treated. A professional dental cleaning combined with regular dental care at home can usually address the problem. Without treatment, however, gingivitis can progress into periodontal disease and eventually contribute to tooth loss.

Sometimes the mouth isn't where the problem starts. Digestive conditions can also affect the way a dog's breath smells.

Gastroenteritis, acid reflux, food intolerances, intestinal blockages, and even gastrointestinal cancer can all be associated with changes in breath odor. Many of these conditions can cause vomiting, which leaves behind a sharp, sour smell from bile.

Acid reflux can also produce a similar sour odor even when a dog isn't actually vomiting.

What a dog eats can have a noticeable effect on breath. It's perfectly normal for some of the smell of a dog's food to linger after a meal, but certain diets can leave a much stronger odor behind.

Seafood and fish oil supplements, for example, can give a dog's breath a distinctly fishy smell. Dogs that eat feces, whether their own or another animal's, can also develop particularly foul breath afterward. This behavior, known as coprophagia, is unpleasant but fairly common.

Bad breath isn't always caused by the teeth or gums. The oral cavity also includes the jaw bones, tongue, soft palate, and the inside of the cheeks, and problems affecting any of these areas can produce an unpleasant smell.

Injuries can become infected and lead to tissue damage, creating the odor associated with the breakdown of damaged tissue. Tumors can also develop in these areas and may cause similar tissue damage and bad breath.

A sweet or fruity smell coming from a dog's breath can have a very different explanation. In a diabetic dog, it can be a sign of ketoacidosis, a serious complication that occurs when the body doesn't have enough insulin and begins burning fat for energy instead.

This process produces ketones, which can become toxic as they accumulate in the blood. The resulting breath can have a sweet, fruity smell that is sometimes compared with acetone.

Interestingly, not everyone can smell ketones on a dog's breath. Differences in how people perceive smells, including genetic differences in scent perception, may explain why the odor is more noticeable to some people than others.

Kidney disease can give a dog's breath a distinct ammonia-like smell.

Healthy kidneys filter waste products such as urea from the bloodstream so they can be removed from the body through urine. When kidney function is impaired, urea can build up in the blood instead.

That excess urea eventually reacts with saliva and converts to ammonia, producing the distinctive smell that can be noticeable on a dog's breath.

An unpleasant smell coming from a dog's mouth doesn't always originate anywhere near the mouth. In fact, the problem could be at the opposite end!

Impacted or infected anal glands can cause a dog to lick or nibble the area in an attempt to relieve the discomfort. Anal gland fluid often has an intensely fishy smell, and when a dog licks the area, that odor can transfer directly to the mouth and breath.

Persistent bad breath is worth investigating rather than simply trying to cover up the smell. The underlying cause could be as manageable as dental disease, but it can also be associated with more serious health problems.

Regular brushing and professional dental cleanings can help prevent periodontal disease, which is the most common cause of ongoing bad breath in dogs.

A sudden change in breath odor deserves particular attention, especially if it appears alongside other changes such as appetite problems, vomiting, or repeated licking at a particular part of the body. In those situations, a vet can help determine what's causing the smell and whether anything else needs to be treated.
